10515-rhymes-of-a-roughneck:
Pat O'Cotter published this verse book in 1918, dedicating it to Alaska, home of the tin can and dog, waste of snow, ice, and moss. O'Cotter calls Alaska the graveyard of ambitions and the by-word for hell, where men come for gold, stick because they cannot leave, and dig, drink, and die. The tone is rough, comic, and bitter.

Poems treat the birth of the land, a woman, a dog, and a walnut tree, the malamute, the prospector, and flotsam, with titles like Unsatisfied and How Long. Roughneck speech and frontier humor fill the verses. Readers get a vivid, Alaskan gold-rush collection, full of hardship, jokes, and hard truth.
1211-a-selection-from-the-lyrical-poems-:
Robert Herrick, a seventeenth-century Devon parson, wrote short, musical lyrics on flowers, maids, wine, and the fleeting hour, and this selection gathers his best. "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may" crowns a book of carpe diem songs, love poems, and country blessings.

Herrick's verse is light, clear, and full of classical grace, with a parson's eye for parish life. The selection trims his bulk to the finest pieces. The book gives an easy door into one of England's most delightful lyric poets, and it suits readers who love short poems well made.
12256-mistress-penwick:
Dutton Payne wrote Mistress Penwick as a historical romance, opening with an Ursuline convent losing a pupil and moving through balls, proposals, and a castle and monastery. The heroine, a beautiful young woman of modest estate, is drawn toward court favor and royal notice.

Chapters follow the Lord of Crandlemar, Sir Julian Pomphrey, Jacques Dempsy, and Lady Constance, with scenes in a butlery, a chapel belfry, and an ancient monastery. The heroine must choose between court ambition, love, and confession, while Lord Cedric forbids her monastery visits. Payne writes in the romantic manner of the period, with intrigue, honor, and faith as competing claims. The novel suits readers who enjoy costume romance with a religious edge.
1231-on-the-track:
Henry Lawson, the voice of the Australian bush, gathers stories of men on the track: swagmen, shearers, and selectors tramping between jobs, telling yarns by campfires. The tales are plain, funny, and often sad, with mateship and hardship as their twin themes.

Lawson writes the bush without romance: drought, debt, and loneliness press on every page, but humor breaks through. The book helped make the short story Australia's own form. It suits readers who like spare, true tales of working life. Lawson's plain tales still stand as the truest short fiction of the bush.
12509-the-moon-rock:
Arthur J. Rees's 1922 mystery, The Moon Rock, opens at a funeral in a bleak Cornish churchyard, where Mrs. Turold is laid among strangers, far from birth and kindred. A Swinburne verse fronts the book, bitter as a tear, and the clergyman's final prayer leaves mourners to turn away. Mrs. Turold, a nonentity in life, is no less in death.

Her husband, family and a moon rock of the title soon draw a detective story from that quiet grave, as Cornish coast, class and old secrets entangle. Rees writes in a traditional mystery manner, with atmosphere and slow revelation. The novel offers a classic 1920s puzzle, where a funeral opens a case rather than closing a life.
12773-mr-prohack:
Arnold Bennett's novel Mr. Prohack follows Arthur Charles Prohack, a punctual Treasury man whose orderly life breaks open. Chapters titled The New Poor, The Theory of Idleness, and The Practice of Idleness trace his experiment: what happens when a careful man stops hurrying and starts living? Family, money, and a yacht all enter the plot.

Prohack hates nothing more than being hurried, and Bennett mines comedy from his war against the clock. His wife Eve, daughter Sissie, and a stream of visitors test his new creed. The novel is witty, humane satire on work, leisure, and middle-class respectability in post-war London.
13355-happy-jack:
Thornton W. Burgess tells the woodland adventures of Happy Jack, a grey squirrel, in this 1918 children's book with pictures by Harrison Cady. Happy Jack drops a nut, quarrels with Chatterer the red squirrel, suspects Striped Chipmunk, and spies on him through the Green Forest.

Feasts, tricks, and small reconciliations follow. Striped Chipmunk shares fat hickory nuts without a quarrel, and Happy Jack begs nuts from Farmer Brown's boy, afraid to step inside a window lest it shut and trap him. Dedicated to William T. Hornaday, champion of American wild life, the book teaches woodland ways through animal talk and gentle humour.
1389-gobseck:
Set in Paris salons of 1829, this short Balzac tale opens with a mother warning her daughter against a young count whose family fortunes are in doubt. The family lawyer Derville then tells the story behind the warning, and the cold figure at its heart is Gobseck, a moneylender who lends at high rates to rich and poor alike.

Through Derville, readers see Gobseck at work among spendthrift heirs, ruined wives, and desperate borrowers, and learn how his loans bind whole families. The tale ends with the strange hoard found in his rooms after his death. It is a sharp study of debt, greed, and the price of living beyond one's means.
14222-poor-jack:
Captain Marryat's Poor Jack, volume ten of his works, follows a Thames boy through temptation, work, and war. Illustrations show Anderson reading Bible and battle news, Jack's father landing after the Nile, Jack aboard an Indiaman, and Bramble saving Bessie. Fisher's Alley, Nanny's room, and the fore-peak yarn all belong to a sailor's London and sea life.

Conscience drives the early chapters. Jack pockets fifteen shillings, creeps to bed without prayers, and wakes dissatisfied, wishing the coins out of his pocket. Old Nanny and old Anderson offer rival counsel, and pride changes his course. Later, as a prisoner in France, Jack escapes with fire and water as agents, while twelve invalids guard forty-seven prisoners at Morlaix and a mayor locks them in an old church. Sea yarn, humor, and moral growth make a classic boys' book for grown readers too.
14814-the-tale-of-jemima-puddle-duck:
Beatrix Potter's 1908 farmyard tale follows Jemima Puddle-duck, annoyed because the farmer's wife will not let her hatch her own eggs. Her sister-in-law, Mrs. Rebeccah Puddle-duck, is glad to leave hatching to someone else, warning that Jemima lacks patience to sit on a nest for twenty-eight days.

Jemima insists she will hatch them all by herself, and sets off to find a nesting place away from the farmyard. Potter's pictures and plain sentences carry the comedy and the danger of that choice. A farmyard tale for Ralph and Betsy, it remains a favourite first story about wanting independence and learning its cost.
14831-andy-grant-s-pluck:
Horatio Alger Jr., author of about seventy boys' books, tells how Andy Grant rises by pluck, honesty and hard work. Alger was born in Revere, Massachusetts, in 1834. A Harvard graduate turned New York writer, he made Ragged Dick his first success and built a career on poor boys who earn their way up.

Andy faces setbacks, false friends and chances that reward steady effort rather than luck alone. Work, thrift and a good name carry him through, while older helpers and rivals test his character. The story follows Alger's familiar pattern, but it does so with pace and warmth. For young readers then and now, it is a plain tale of grit in a city that rewards it.
15158-in-time-of-emergency-a-citizen-s-h:
Issued by the Department of Defense, Office of Civil Defense, this citizen handbook prepares American families for nuclear attack and natural disasters. Blank lines at the front ask each owner to record a fallout shelter, school and workplace shelters, and emergency phone numbers for police, fire, doctors, and hospitals.

Inside, plain instructions cover warning signals, shelter, food, water, first aid, and what to do after an attack or storm. The tone is calm, practical, and official, meant to be kept at home and used in fear. As a Cold War document, the book shows how the state taught ordinary people to face unthinkable danger.
15569-the-cuckoo-clock:
Mrs. Molesworth published this children's fantasy in London and New York in 1895, illustrated by Walter Crane. It is dedicated to Mary Josephine and to the memory of her brother Thomas Grindal, both friendly little critics of the author's children's stories. An Edinburgh note dated 1877 heads the dedication, marking an earlier origin.

Eleven chapters follow Griselda in an old house, set back from a village street, through the country of the nodding mandarins, pictures, butterfly land, and the other side of the moon. A cuckoo clock, a little boat, and a farewell of cuckoo, cuckoo, goodbye, give the tale its magic frame. Molesworth writes gentle fantasy for children, where obedience, patience, and wonder lead a girl through strange lands and safely home.
16274-the-life-and-adventures-of-kit-car:
De Witt C. Peters, late assistant surgeon in the United States Army, published this life of Kit Carson in New York in 1858, from facts narrated by Carson himself. Original illustrations drawn by Lumley show Kit with his favorite horse Apache, and the dedication honors Colonel Ceran St. Vrain of New Mexico, among the first Americans on the Rocky Mountains and an early discoverer of Carson's energy and courage.

Carson's long life as trapper, guide, and scout unfolds through mountains, deserts, and frontier settlements, crowned, Peters says, with honorable achievement. The book helped fix Carson as the Nestor, or wise elder, of the Rockies in popular memory. Readers of Western history will find a lively, heroic early biography.
16541-poor-man-s-rock:
Bertrand W. Sinclair's 1920 novel opens on the Gulf of Georgia in August sun, an immense empty stretch of water. The prologue, Long, Long Ago, leads to the house in Cradle Bay, his own country, sea boots and salmon, vested rights, and peril of the sea. Hearts are not always trumps, business as usual, and top dog mark the later chapters.

Sinclair writes of British Columbia's coast with knowledge of boats, fish, and hard bargains. The tale mixes family saga with sea adventure. Readers of Pacific Northwest fiction will find a strong, salty novel of a man, a rock, and the life built upon it.
1668-the-tapestried-chamber-and-death-of:
Sir Walter Scott pairs two short tales in this volume, both drawn from the storytelling tradition of the Scottish Borders. In the first, a guest sleeps in a tapestried chamber of an old house and meets something in the night that no daylight explanation quite covers.

The second, The Death of the Laird's Jock, turns to border warfare and a father's grief after a feud. Scott frames both stories as things told to him by others. That fireside manner is part of their effect: brief, local, and haunted by a past that the present has not fully laid to rest.
16731-the-garden-of-the-plynck:
Karle Wilson Baker wrote this children's fantasy of Sara and the Garden of the Plynck. Chapters move from the Dimplesmithy and Avrillia, through invaders, crumbs and waffles, a lost laugh, and the Vale of Tears, to cheers and butter and Sara's day. It opens with a complaint about grown folk who start tales of when they were little, then stop with a moral.

Baker writes for children in a warm, teasing voice, with a garden world full of odd folk and small wonders. Sara learns through play, loss, and laughter, not through lectures. Young readers get a gentle, old-style fantasy, best read aloud, with a heroine who thinks for herself and a world that rewards kind curiosity.
17277-the-story-of-a-monkey-on-a-stick:
Laura Lee Hope's 1920 Make Believe story follows a toy monkey on a stick who wakes in a pasteboard box, far from the toy store where he slept. He rubs his nose, wonders at the strange place, and sets out on small adventures: school, a janitor's house, a queer ride, monkeyshines, a cave, rain, a tent, and a show. Herbert at last finds the monkey and gives the tale its heart.

Hope writes for very young readers, with short chapters and a toy hero who feels and talks like a child. Harry L. Smith's pictures match the fun step by step. The book suits bedtime reading, and it charms children who love toys that come alive when no one watches.
1764-billy-and-the-big-stick:
Richard Harding Davis sets this story in Haiti, where the Wilmot Electric Light Company has lit the unpaved streets of Port-au-Prince and, as a by-product, tried to make money. Billy, left in charge of the company's interests, finds himself dealing with police, politicians, and a stranger who helps himself to Billy's pipe and tobacco with cheerful nerve.

The tale turns on American business abroad and the big stick behind it, and Davis keeps the tone comic even as the stakes rise. It is a period piece about gunboat diplomacy in miniature: a young American and a small republic. The bargain is struck in a room where everyone knows who holds the power.
17842-dead-man-s-rock:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, known as Q, wrote this romance, published in 1887 and prepared here from an 1894 edition, dedicating it to the memory of his father. Book one, the quest of the great ruby, opens with the strange will of the narrator's grandfather, Amos Trenoweth. The narrator's father goes to seek the treasure, while his mother hears a cry in the night.

Two strange men watch the sea on Polkimbra beach, a song is sung, and a knife is drawn on Dead Man's Rock. The sailor Georgio Rhodon enters the tale. Readers get a Cornish treasure romance, brisk and atmospheric, from the future Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch. The book suits readers of adventure and of Q's early fiction.
18356-orange-and-green-a-tale-of-the-boy:
G. A. Henty wrote this tale of the Boyne and Limerick for young readers. Henty's preface notes that Ireland had for years been prominent in public attention, and that recent discontent had its root in an old sense of grievance. The novel carries a young hero through the wars that set James against William in Ireland.

Chapters open with a shipwreck, then ask for James or William, bring the king in Ireland, and follow the siege and relief of Derry. Dundalk, the coming battle, Boyne Water, pleasant quarters, and a cavalry raid follow, with the first siege of Limerick, winter quarters, a dangerous mission, Athlone, and peace. Readers get Henty's Irish history as adventure: sieges, battles, and a lad learning which side honor lies on.
18522-the-wreck:
A children's story published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1880, The Wreck opens in a grove behind an old farmhouse, where Ollie has been swinging for nearly an hour. Her mother calls from the back door, basket in hand, looking for her all over the house. Ollie jumps down, leaves the swing to die away by itself, and skips up the path to see what her mother wants.

Mrs. Rogers needs more sugar for new cookies, and Ollie takes the basket to run the errand. Willie, looking through the window, would like a walk, but the doctor says he must not leave the house before next week. Ollie throws him a kiss and starts down the path, when a rat-tat-tat sounds behind her. Young readers get a domestic tale for little children: a swing, an errand, and the small excitements of a farmhouse day.
18700-the-mayor-of-warwick:
Herbert M. Hopkins published this novel with Houghton, Mifflin in 1906, setting it at St. George's Hall, a college on a hill above the city of Warwick. The hall's castellated tower, arched doorway, and vine-hung windows recall Oxford and Cambridge, though only one side of its planned quadrangle stands built.

Chapters follow a meeting in a maple walk, the bishop's daughter, and a candidate for office. A mayor who at last finds himself anchors the tale, with family furniture, confessions, and town politics along the way. The book mixes college life, romance, and civic ambition in an old-England-looking town made new in America. Its closing chapters bring father and daughter, mayor and townsfolk, toward a settled understanding.
18817-ralestone-luck:
André Norton's adventure, published by Appleton-Century in 1938 with pictures by James Reid, brings the Ralestones home to Pirate's Haven. Val, Ricky, and Rupert, still Marquess of Lorne after two hundred years in America, count themselves among the New Poor, stopping a roadster to reckon five gallons of gas.

Their luck runs in rhyme: "by the oak leaf, by the sea wave, by the broadsword blade, thus hold we Lorne." When leaf, wave, and blade are dust and rust, the rhyme answers: by our luck. Chapters bring an unobtrusive visitor, pistols for two and coffee for one, a tenant's discovery, great-uncle Rick walking the hall, a swamp, and pirate ways hidden ways. The Ralestones stand together against the past's claims.
20119-ambrotox-and-limping-dick:
Ambrotox and Limping Dick is a novel that opens in a fine English garden at noon. Amaryllis Caldegard sits under a cedar tree on Bellamy's south lawn. A piece of needlework and three fresh novels lie on her table. Yet for a full hour she has neither sewn nor read a line.

That still, warm scene hints at a mind fixed on other things. Love, secrets, and country house life drive tales of this kind. The odd title pairs a strange name with a limping Dick. Readers get a period romance where calm lawns hide sharp turns ahead.
20323-that-stick:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote That Stick, a novel of a quiet country town. Two dignified elderly ladies in black silk walk a calm street. A man of about forty hurries up to speak with them. His usually pale cheeks are flushed, and he comes breathlessly toward them.

He has the air of a managing clerk with urgent business. Yonge, a famed Victorian novelist, finds drama in such small encounters. Church, family, and duty shape the lives behind that hurried talk. Readers get Yonge's keen eye for manners, conscience, and quiet English life.
20788-storm-over-warlock:
Shann Lantee watches a Throg attack burn below his shelf of rock in Storm over Warlock. Hearing of Throg cruelty is one thing, Andre Norton writes, and seeing it is quite another. Shann shakes in his Survey Corps uniform, pinned by more than mere care.

Norton strands a young scout on a wild world where witches hold real power. Beasts, alien foes, and strange gifts test him at each turn. Her tales of lone youths on far worlds won a vast, loyal readership. This book shows her gift for brisk plots, lean prose, and worlds that feel lived in.
20837-peggy-in-her-blue-frock:
Alice shows her dimples as she takes books from the lowest shelf at home. Two years younger than Peggy, she fears the stepladder and keeps low. Eliza Orne White sets the sisters side by side in Peggy in Her Blue Frock.

White wrote warm tales of New England family life for children. Peggy, large for her age, leads with spirit while Alice follows sweetly. Small deeds, school days, and home joys fill the gentle plot. The book shows White's gift for making plain days feel rich, a gift that won her a loyal place in children's reading.
21575-poor-jack:
Tom Saunders, called Poor Jack, dates his birth to 1786 in Captain Marryat's Poor Jack of 1840. His father ties the year to the Druids being turned over to the Melpomene. Jack checks the tale and finds that event fell in January 1787.

Greenwich and the Thames banks form the book's world, as in Jacob Faithful. Many landmarks Marryat names still stand, though their uses have changed. Jack's rise from river boy to pilot is told with warmth and close detail. The book, Marryat's sixteenth, stays a loved and lasting portrait of old watermen's London and its river folk.
21756-philosopher-jack:
Jack, called Philosopher by his college friends, is nineteen and full of hard questions as this Ballantyne tale opens. His closest friend gives advice in just two words: Do, or Don't. Jack, whose other name is Edwin, argues with everyone, himself most of all. Sitting at his desk, he asks in bitterness why he was ever born.

Ballantyne takes this restless student out of his room and into a life that tests his thinking. Talk must give way to action, and fine ideas must survive rough seas and hard work. The tale mixes college humor with the author's steady moral hand. Jack's search for a reason to live gives the adventure its weight.
21854-the-woman-in-black:
A financier's murder starts this detective novel by E. C. Bentley, published in 1913 and dedicated to G. K. Chesterton. Sigsbee Manderson's scheming brain is scattered by a shot from an unknown hand. Bentley's dedication letter jokes that his only noble motive was Chesterton's pleasure, and that he owed him a book for The Man Who Was Thursday. Hamlet's words on purposes mistook head the tale.

The Woman in Black is better known in crime history as Trent's Last Case, the tale of painter-detective Philip Trent. Bentley reshaped the detective story by letting his hero reason brilliantly toward a wrong answer. The book became a landmark of the genre. Elegant, ironic, and humane, it still anchors lists of the great detective novels.
21942-dickory-dock:
A baby, a mongrel dog, and two children make the household of L. T. Meade's Dickory Dock, published about 1890. The baby is small and not particularly fair, but it has round limbs, a dimple, and a soft, half-pathetic look in its blue eyes. Its mother died at its birth, and the orphan was carried to an uncle's house. A nurse washes and feeds it in the background, but the children and the dog are its true caretakers.

They call up its smiles and keep its small world warm. Meade, author of A World of Girls, writes childhood with a practiced, tender hand. Mrs. Franklin, tall and fretful, speaks for the grown world's worries. The tale is gentle Victorian domestic fiction built around one helpless child.
22109-the-black-wolf-pack: The Black Wolf Pack is a boys' adventure novel told in the first person by a young narrator. He opens by skipping school errands at speed: a roadster, a pile of library books, and a list of jobs from Mrs. Crawford. Home and downtown pull him in two directions at once. The everyday bustle soon gives way to the outdoor mystery promised by the title.
23049-old-jack:
An old sailor tells his life in Old Jack. The narrator took an early opportunity of making Old Jack's acquaintance, for such, he says, was the name by which the man was best known. Without reluctance Jack gave his history. It is now presented to the public with certain corrections, with which younger readers, the editor trusts, will find no fault.

Sea stories told by veterans filled the magazines this tale came from. Jack's career runs through the age of sail, its storms, ports, and shipmates rendered in yarn-spinning form. The editor's light hand keeps the salt in the speech. Such pieces taught landsmen the sea's vocabulary and its hard code of luck. Old Jack himself, weathered and willing, carries the whole cargo.
23115-the-billow-and-the-rock:
Scotland's union divides opinion in The Billow and the Rock. The Union was still new when the tale opens. Scotland's wisest heads saw safety only under a king and parliament shared with England. Many great men disagreed, preferring no rule over themselves and unchecked power over their dependents.

Against that politics of lairds and loyalty, the story sets its billow and its rock, the sea's force and the faith that withstands it. Scottish tales of the Union years mixed covenant, clan, and coast in just this way. The opening argument is unusually direct, a small history lesson before the drama. Readers get both, the politics of 1707 and a tale built to make them felt.
23272-the-story-of-the-rock:
The Story of the Rock tells how a famous lighthouse was built. Its builders used one plain fact: stone outweighs timber, so a stone tower carries the weight that wind and water demand. That added weight steadied the tower against wind and water.

The plan worked. The lighthouse was not only a success at the time, it has lasted well over two centuries. Ever since its completion, it has been a highly regarded model of lighthouse building. Readers get an engineering story in plain terms: one smart choice about materials, tested by two hundred years of storms.
23439-attention-saint-patrick:
Murray Leinster, pen name of William Fitzgerald Jenkins, wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in nineteen sixty, about a planet named Eire. President O'Hanrahan of the planetary government listens, unhappily, to an official guest from Earth.

Sean O'Donohue, chair of the Dail committee on the planet's condition, is short, opinionated, and sharp eyed, and he could cut off all support from the still struggling colony if he chose. Leinster plays the meeting for comedy and for legend, as old tales bend in the passage of time and space. Readers who like sly, Irish flavoured science fiction will enjoy the clash of colony pride, Earth politics, and saints both old and new.
23534-or-your-money-back:
David Gordon wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in September nineteen fifty nine, about a man whose advice proves stronger than he knows. The narrator hears out Jason Howley, a lean, slope shouldered man with a gadget, trying to look both interested and co operative, as good business demands.

Neither Howley nor his gadget impresses him at first. The case turns on things deemed acceptable precisely because they do not work, and everyone knows they really do not. Gordon plays the joke with dry wit, as a salesman's patter meets a device that may work all too well. Readers who like sly, idea driven science fiction will enjoy the tale's twist on guarantees, gadgets, and the price of being believed.
23773-the-coming-wave-or-the-hidden-trea:
Oliver Optic published The Coming Wave in 1874, the fourth volume of his Yacht Club Series and an entirely independent story. Though its incidents lie on Penobscot Bay and concern boats and yachting, its characters are new, and the book promises breezy sailing.

The hidden treasure of High Rock gives the plot its pull, and Leopold on the lookout watches from the frontispiece. Young sailors, yacht clubs, and Maine waters fill the chapters, in Optic's brisk, instructive manner. For readers who like boats, it is a fine entry point to the series, needing no knowledge of the earlier volumes.
24180-alarm-clock:
Everett B. Cole wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science Fiction in September 1960, with pictures by Van Dongen. It opens at Opertal Prison, where years of feet have polished the courtyard stones until the setting sun reflects from them like mosaic. Stan Graham crosses from the library to the cell block, past coarse, weathered walls whose severe lines recall Kendall Hall at the Stellar Guard Academy.

Cole frames the tale with high explosives such as ammonium nitrate, violent once triggered yet seemingly inert under beating and burning until the one required shock arrives. People rarely leave Opertal against their wishes, and few wish to stay. Readers get a prison story built on a trigger waiting for its shock.
24277-card-trick:
Walter Bupp wrote this science fiction story for Analog in January 1961, with pictures by Douglas. The game is stud, with seven at the table and Nick banking it, all wearing the beat look of compulsive gamblers behind attempted poker faces. A skinny, sharp-chinned young gambler warns the table that anyone caught using psi powers to beat the odds must repay double losses.

The narrator, a biochemist for whom DNA should be life's cornerstone, has just been certified Normal that evening by Dr. Shari King, his dinner date. The Psi Lodge, the blurb warns, has ways of applying pressure, but the narrator's peculiar talent is one even they have never heard of. Readers get a poker tale of psi, bluff, and a talent kept close.
24721-operation-haystack:
Frank Herbert wrote this short science-fiction story, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1959 and illustrated by van Dongen. Its hero is Lewis Orne, an Investigation and Adjustment scout, whose problem is tougher than ferreting out fanatics, or even spotting a genetic line of dedicated men.

Orne lands on Marak carrying a dying man, alive only in a womblike creche pod that has taken over his vital functions. Herbert, later famous for Dune, builds a tale of intrigue, loyalty, and hidden purpose. Readers get a tense, clever story of a scout facing a conspiracy he can barely name.
25073-overbeck:
Johann Friedrich Overbeck, written by J. Beavington Atkinson for the Illustrated Biographies of the Great Artists series, traces a German painter who helped found the Nazarene movement in Rome. Overbeck rejected the academic art of his day and turned instead to early Italian religious painting as his model.

Atkinson follows Overbeck from his youth in Lübeck through his years in Rome, his fresco work, and his long career painting sacred subjects in a deliberately simple, devout style. Engravings illustrate key works, and the life doubles as a short history of a movement that prized faith and craft over fashionable display.
25090-the-tale-of-billy-woodchuck:
Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Billy Woodchuck, part of the Sleepy-Time Tales series published in 1916, is a gentle animal story for young children. Billy, a young woodchuck, learns about the meadow, the farm, and the woods around his burrow through small adventures and meetings with other animals.

Each chapter offers a short, self-contained episode with a simple lesson about caution, kindness, or hard work. Bailey's plain sentences and familiar farmyard world made the series a bedtime favorite, and the book still reads as a warm introduction to nature for early readers.
25316-frank-merriwell-s-son-or-a-chip-of:
Burt L. Standish's Frank Merriwell's Son, published by Street and Smith in 1906, is number 137 in the Merriwell series. The chip off the old block faces a new life, a birthmark, and a maid of mystery. A face in a watch, substitutes, a moonlight meeting, and a kidnapping follow along the way.

At Merry Home in Bloomfield, Frank Merriwell himself meets the train with carriages, and old friends greet their former leader. Juanita, watching a rival woman, whispers that this is the woman. Standish delivers the school-and-sport adventure his readers expected, with loyalty and pluck rewarded.
25921-the-long-trick:
Bartimeus, pen name of Captain Lewis Anselm da Costa Ritchie of the Royal Navy, tells naval life in the Great War in this 1917 book. Chapters run from back from the land and the navy special to Ultima Thule. War babies, Uncle Bill, wet bobs, and carrying on follow, with sweethearts and wives, the battle of the mist, and the aftermath. Two chapters first ran in Blackwood's Magazine.

The book opens in London fog, thick as a pall over the city, and moves to ships, periscopes, and games of peep bo with the foe. A watch officer slews his periscope past floating hay bales, glad they will not dent the glass, and laughs that he sees the enemy who cannot see him. Dedicated to Chunks, also called Hunks, Tunks, Tinks, or Tonks, the book mixes humor and war's strain.
25959-littlebourne-lock:
F. Bayford Harrison sets a Thames tale of a lock house, a lost child, and a better life, printed by Blackie and Son. The book opens on a July morning mist over the river, with larks singing above and sun shining through. Edward Rowles, the lock keeper, steps from his house, overgrown with honeysuckle and clematis, to look up and down the stream and at the weir where water tumbles and roars.

Chapters move from number 103 and Juliet Mitchell to a pretty churchyard, a river trip, a child missing and found, and a thorough change. One scene counts the cost of a winter mantle in shillings and pence, down to braid, buttons, and seven shillings for the making, to prove thrift beats ninepence piecework. The tale is gentle, English, and fond of river life.
25985-bardell-v-pickwick:
Percy Fitzgerald edits the trial of Bardell v. Pickwick, the breach of promise case from Dickens's Pickwick Papers, with notes and commentaries, printed by Elliot Stock in 1902. The case, tried at Guildhall on April 1, 1828, before Mr. Justice Stareleigh and a special jury, is better known than many real trials, Fitzgerald says. Readers know the judge, counsel such as Sergeant Buzfuz, the witnesses, and of course plaintiff and defendant.

Fitzgerald sketches Mr. Justice Gaselee, original of Stareleigh, from a family portrait. Court scenes show Jackson serving subpoenas, Pickwick's disgust at his unwelcome visitor, and Sam Weller answering in composed style. The book treats a comic fiction trial with legal care, and its humors still read fresh after seventy years.
26165-lady-luck:
Hugh Wiley's Lady Luck, published by Alfred A. Knopf in 1921, follows the Wildcat, a Southern ex-soldier back from the war, and his goat mascot Lily. The book opens at the Memphis station, where the Wildcat haggles over coffee, collects Captain Jack's bed-roll, and hires an express wagon for a ride into town. His talk runs in dialect, full of jokes about officers, helmets, and the war he is glad to forget.

Later scenes bring a ouija board party, where a hostess named Cuspidora Lee defends her spirits against charges of lying. The Wildcat's questions about a man called Honey Tone stir fresh trouble. The book offers comic, vernacular tales of a veteran finding his footing at home, with luck, good and bad, waiting round each bend.
26348-lisbeth-longfrock:
Hans Aanrud's Lisbeth Longfrock, translated from Norwegian by Laura E. Poulsson and illustrated by Othar Holmboe, appeared from Ginn and Company in 1907. It opens at Hoel Farm on a clear, cold day near spring, where Bearhunter the shaggy dog guards pigs and goats while his paws ache with cold. Lisbeth arrives to work on the farm, starting as a spinning woman.

Chapters follow spring pasture, summer at the saeter, the taming of Crookhorn, and home from the mountain dairy. Glory Peak, a visit to Peerout Castle, Sunday at the saeter, and Lisbeth's rise to head milkmaid complete the year. When herder boys lose their flocks at play, Lisbeth gathers them, knowing the disgrace of a lost flock. The book gives Norwegian farm life in warm detail.
26569-monkey-on-his-back:
Charles V. De Vet published this science-fiction story in Galaxy magazine in June 1960. It opens with a man walking a long glass-walled corridor with a blue knapsack, unsure who he is or what he is doing there. Pursued through a terminal-like hall, he hides a flat briefcase in a pay locker and slides the key under it before his captors seize him.

The scene shifts to a psychoanalyst's office, where Milton Bergstrom questions John Zarwell about what he talked of while under. Zarwell reenacts chases and a village being ravaged, moving among dying men without quite taking part. The title's monkey is the burden of cast-off identities, and the story asks which of Zarwell's selves is truly his own.
26647-nuts-for-future-historians-to-crac:
Horace W. Smith collected and published this documentary volume at Philadelphia in 1856, containing the Cadwalader pamphlet, Valley Forge letters, and more. Smith had been gathering material for a life of his great-grandfather, the Reverend William Smith, provost of the University of Pennsylvania, when he read W. B. Reed's life of General Joseph Reed. Reed's remarks on Smith struck him as uncalled for, ungentlemanly, and untrue.

Rather than answer in kind inside the biography, Smith printed the historical facts about Reed in a small volume by itself, in an edition meant to survive buying up and destruction. The book also weighs Irving's life of Washington, correcting its estimate of Reed and its Major Stobo error. It is a partisan archive, offered as nuts for future historians to crack.
26985-killykinick:
Mary T. Waggaman's 1917 school story opens the week after Commencement at Saint Andrew's, where the halls have gone silent and only the left overs remain. These are the boys who must spend the summer at school, and they work off their steam on the flying trapeze and the high bar.

Among them are Jim Norris and Dud Fielding, both fourteen, and little Fred Neville, left at Saint Andrew's since age five in a priestly uncle's care. The tale follows their summer of scrapes and loyalties, told in the warm Catholic school-story style Waggaman's readers knew from Billy Boy and Tommy Travers.
27111-history-of-new-brunswick:
Peter Fisher's History of New Brunswick, first published in 1825 and reprinted in 1921 under the New Brunswick Historical Society, tells the province's early story. Settled mainly by Loyalist families torn by the American Revolution, the province was constituted separately forty-three years before Fisher wrote.

Fisher traces a people who abandoned homes and all for high ideals of national duty, then built political institutions and industrial life in a northern wilderness. The reprint adds explanatory notes, preserving the first historical work on a province built by sacrifice. Fisher's work was the first historical work on the province, in the Historical Society's opinion.
28016-in-the-tail-of-the-peacock:
Isabel Savory, author of A Sportswoman in India, published In the Tail of the Peacock in London with Hutchinson and Company in 1903, with forty-eight illustrations from photographs. The Moorish proverb of the title says the earth is a peacock and Morocco is its tail.

Savory warns that the book holds no thrilling adventures or days devoted to sport, only wandering, idleness, and quiet observation, from Tangier and Tetuan through caravanserais, Moorish houses, and cemeteries. The preface invites readers who enjoy waste places, trifling incidents, and human natures remote from their own.
28032-sprays-of-shamrock:
Clinton Scollard's Sprays of Shamrock, printed at Portland, Maine, in 1914, is a book of short poems about Ireland. Scollard writes of hills, lakes, small towns, and holy wells, naming places from Kerry and Donegal to Sligo and Derry. His lines praise the land itself rather than its long list of wrongs.

Many poems are songs of exile, homecoming, and love, with a few ballads of old chiefs and rebels. The tone stays lyrical and fond, even when a poem recalls loss or parting. The book offers a compact, musical portrait of Ireland as an American poet of Irish feeling saw it.
28565-good-luck:
Mrs. L. T. Meade's Good Luck, published in Chicago in 1896, opens in the London Hospital's out-patients' department, on a foggy day toward the end of November. Among the waiting crowd stands an old, cherry-cheeked woman with bright blue eyes, snow-white fluffy hair, and a neat black dress and shawl.

Her hand pains her right up to the shoulder, and she cannot hold her needle, which threatens her living as a needleworker. She bears her trouble cheerfully, chatting with neighbours about their babies and their ills while she waits for the doctor. Meade's novel follows this little woman's fortunes, and its title hints at the luck, good and bad, that shapes her life.
28619-the-cuckoo-clock:
Mrs. Molesworth's The Cuckoo Clock, published by J. B. Lippincott of Philadelphia and London with color illustrations by Maria L. Kirk, belongs to the Stories All Children Love set. Its dedication, dated Edinburgh 1877, addresses Mary Josephine and the memory of her brother Thomas Grindal, friendly little critics of children's stories. The book stands beside Heidi, Pinocchio, and The Water Babies in the series.

The tale opens in a very old house on an old street in an old town, belonging to a gone-by time. Chapters follow impatient Griselda, obeying orders, the country of the nodding mandarins, pictures, butterfly-land, Master Phil, and the other side of the moon. A legend of Donegal, the castle in the lough, closes the volume.
28725-harding-s-luck:
E. Nesbit's Harding's Luck, published by Frederick A. Stokes of New York in 1910 with sixteen illustrations by H. R. Millar, opens at New Cross. Dickie lives in a row of horrid little houses on a slope where green fields once ran to the river, and Deptford merchants' stately houses stood in pleasant gardens. A wicked giant, Nesbit says, seems to have painted out the green in yellow ochre and mud color.

Miles of houses follow, with no green except cabbages in greengrocers' shops and creeping-jenny on dirty sills. Each house keeps a little yard called the garden, green only to back windows. Chapters promise Tinkler and the moonflower, burglars, escape, buried treasure, kidnapping, a noble deed, and Lord Arden. Readers get a London boy's tale, half street life and half magic.
28955-a-narrative-of-the-mutiny-on-board:
William Lay of Saybrook and Cyrus M. Hussey of Nantucket wrote this 1828 narrative of the mutiny aboard the whaling ship Globe in January 1824, and of two years living on the Mulgrave Islands. Lay and Hussey were the only survivors of the massacre of the ship's company, and they published their account in New London. A vocabulary of island words closes the book.

The narrative gives the mutiny, the killings, and the survivors' life among island people, with observations on manners and customs. Its copyright entry, recorded in October 1827, preserves the full title and the authors' claim. Readers get a grim, firsthand sea tale from the age of sail, valuable both as adventure and as early evidence about Pacific island life.
3126-on-horseback:
Warner rides through the American South in this comic travel sketch. His guide is a Professor who rode for the Union in the Civil War. The man can recite Chaucer on horseback at a trot and never miss an accent. His horsemanship wins notice across North Carolina and part of East Tennessee.

Humor grows from the talk between riders and from the gap between book learning and road sense. The journey meanders from mount to mount and anecdote to anecdote. Readers meet the South at walking pace, through its people, its roads, and the small vanities of men on horseback.
3480-the-hunchback:
James Sheridan Knowles pairs two of his plays in this volume, published by Cassell in 1887. The first, The Hunchback, is a romantic drama of love, disguise, and family secrets, long popular on the Victorian stage. The second, The Love Chase, is a comedy of courtship with a cast led by Sir William Fondlove, Waller, Wildrake, and Lydia.

An introduction sketches Knowles himself, born at Cork in 1784, son of a teacher of elocution related to the Sheridans, who moved to London as a boy and knew Hazlitt and Lamb. The volume suits readers interested in nineteenth century theater, giving two contrasting plays by one of its most successful dramatists.
5143-the-auction-block:
Rex Beach's novel opens with Peter Knight, a Democrat of twenty years, grumbling about politics to his son James in a shabby armchair. From that domestic scene, the story follows the Knight family through New York life, where money, ambition, and marriage are bargained over as sharply as goods at an auction.

Beach, known for Northern adventure tales, turns here to city society, theatre, and the pursuit of success. The novel's title points to its theme: the price people pay, and the price put upon them, when wealth and reputation are on the block. Readers get a brisk early twentieth-century story of family, fortune, and social climbing.
5163-guy-garrick:
Arthur B. Reeve's Guy Garrick, another Craig Kennedy story, opens with a stolen motor and a murder car. The story then moves through a thicket mystery, a liquid bullet, a blackmailer, a gambling den, and a motor bandit. Kennedy's tools include the detectaphone, the vocaphone, and the speaking arc, as he tracks a gang through garages, raids, and newspaper fakes.

The novel shows Reeve at his most gadget-filled, using new inventions to solve old crimes. Readers will find a fast pulp mystery of the motor age, in which cars, telephones. Eavesdropping devices matter as much as the criminal's motive.
528-joe-the-hotel-boy-or-winning-out-by-:
Horatio Alger Jr. follows Joe, a country lad raised by a hermit, in this success tale. After a storm and a ruined home, Joe seeks a blue box, works in a summer hotel, then in a city hotel, facing swindles, mining shares, and a hotel fire. A satchel, a tree, and two evil-doers mark his road.

Alger writes in his plain moral style, praising pluck, honesty, and kind deeds. Joe wins not by luck alone but by standing firm when others cheat. Young readers will find a brisk, hopeful story of a boy who earns his place, step by step, from storm to city.
5417-struggling-upward-or-luke-larkin-s-:
Horatio Alger wrote this rags-to-respectability tale about Luke Larkin, a poor but hardworking young man in the village of Groveton. The story opens on a winter afternoon beside a village pond. A schoolteacher and a group of boys gather there, and a modest Waterbury watch becomes a small prize and a test of character. Luke's honesty and grit are set against boys with easier lives.

Like Alger's other heroes, Luke climbs by steady effort, good conduct, and timely help from older mentors. Setbacks, temptations, and small acts of courage mark each step upward. Young readers get a plain, hopeful story about work, integrity, and the belief that a poor boy can earn his way to a better life.
5844-the-adventures-of-johnny-chuck:
Burgess follows Johnny Chuck, a woodchuck, through a year of restlessness and adventure. Chapters bring gentle Sister South Wind, callers, singers of the Smiling Pool, and Johnny's discovery of who the sweet singers are. Johnny grows dissatisfied, turns tramp, and meets first adventures, another strange chuck, and a reason he did not fight.

Young readers learn woodchuck life through story: burrows, seasons, neighbors, and the urge to wander. Burgess writes in short chapters suited to bedtime, with animal characters who feel like children testing their world. The book suits early readers and read-aloud families, and it continues the Green Meadow tales that made Burgess a beloved children's author.
5846-the-adventures-of-poor-mrs-quack:
Burgess tells the story of Poor Mrs Quack, a duck in trouble, in the Bedtime Story-Books series, illustrated by Harrison Cady. Contents open with Peter Rabbit becoming acquainted with Mrs Quack, who proves distrustful at first, and the story follows her fortunes through marsh and meadow. An illustration shows Peter musing that marshes must be something like swamps.

Young readers greet a mother duck whose worries and wanderings teach patience, kindness, and care for neighbors. Burgess favors gentle humor and clear morals, with Peter Rabbit as a friendly guide. The book suits early readers and bedtime reading, offering a short, tender animal tale where help arrives through friendship rather than force.
588-master-humphrey-s-clock:
Charles Dickens frames tales and sketches round an old clock keeper in this volume, first issued as a weekly miscellany. Master Humphrey, who loves his clock's voice, invites readers to gather as friends while the clock counts hours and cheats them of heaviness. A dedication to poet Samuel Rogers fronts the book.

Dickens writes in warm, bustling prose, mixing humor, pathos, and London scenes. The clock device later gave way to full novels, but these opening pieces show Dickens finding his voice. The book charms as a glimpse of a young master learning to hold a crowd week by week.
6114-the-young-firemen-of-lakeville-or-h:
Frank V. Webster opens The Young Firemen of Lakeville with a midnight alarm, peril, talk, and Bert's plan, then buying an engine and its first run. Bert saves a tramp, the boys work on the lake, and a narrow escape, mysterious actions, and suspicions aroused follow.

Herbert Dare's pluck gives the book its subtitle, and the Lakeville boys learn firefighting as teamwork under pressure. Webster, author of boy books from farm boys to newsboy partners, writes brisk adventure where quick wits and steady nerves matter. The engine, the lake, and the alarm bell drive the tale.
6371-the-purgatory-of-st-patrick:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translates Calderon's Purgatory of St. Patrick fully from Spanish in the metre of the original, in the same 1873 volume as Life is a Dream. The introduction, shared with that volume, calls Calderon's two dramas his most celebrated, played across Europe though little staged in England. Mac-Carthy's verse carries Patrick's prodigies, as earth trembles, air groans in thunder, and sun hides its face before the saint.

Crowds, awe struck, attend Patrick on his way, fearing punishment, and saying he comes to try his spells on them that day. The play's purgatory, a place between north and west on an island, gives the drama its title and its trial. Mac-Carthy keeps Calderon's metre and wonder, so that English readers meet a Spanish saint play as poetry, fierce, marvellous, and confident in miracle.
7165-the-legends-of-saint-patrick:
Aubrey de Vere turns the old tales of Patrick into verse, giving Ireland's patron saint a full book of legends in measured, devout poetry. The volume comes from his collected poems, and its short prose introduction sets the younger De Vere beside his father, Sir Aubrey, whose own poems won praise from Wordsworth. That family line frames the book as work passed down through a house steeped in verse.

Patrick stands at the heart of the poems, and the Irish past around him supplies their colour and weight. Readers meet a saint shaped by story rather than by dry record, with faith, land, and people woven through each telling. The verse keeps a grave, musical tone throughout, suited to tales meant to be read aloud and kept in mind.
7495-to-infidelity-and-back:
Evangelist Henry F. Lutz tells his own religious journey in this autobiography, published at Cincinnati in 1911. Its subtitle says the story plainly: how I found Christ and his church. Lutz frames the journey with a ship's image. Religion is the ship, faith in God the pole-star, free will the rudder, and conscience the compass. Jesus Christ is the pilot, steering by the Word of God rather than the creeds and opinions of men.

Quoting Bacon, that slight tastes of philosophy may move one to atheism while fuller draughts lead back to religion, Lutz traces his passage from unbelief to faith. The book is dedicated to the pioneers of the great restoration movement. It speaks to truth-seekers in his own earnest, plainspoken voice, as one who has made the voyage himself.
7896-the-eight-strokes-of-the-clock:
Maurice Leblanc's The Eight Strokes of the Clock presents eight adventures told, he claims, by Arsene Lupin as if they befell a friend, Prince Renine. Leblanc admits he can hardly tell the two apart, given the hero's actions, behavior, and character, and leaves readers to judge.

Contents run from the top of a tower and a water bottle through Jean Louis and a tell-tale film. Therese and Germaine, a lady with a hatchet, footprints in snow, and the sign of Mercury follow. Hortense Daniel whispers to Rossigny from a window as the first mystery opens.
865-passing-of-the-third-floor-back:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this tale of a Bloomsbury lodging house, where tenants live side by side in suspicion and spite. One November afternoon, a stranger takes the third-floor back room, a modest man whose quiet kindness slowly alters the house. Each lodger, from the landlady down, finds a hidden good stirred to life.

Jerome tells the story with gentle humour and a moral touch, without preaching it flat. The stranger passes through, and the house is changed by his passing. The tale, first published in 1908, has lasted as a favourite fable of kindness, and as a showcase for Jerome's warm, humane comedy.
8879-there-back:
George MacDonald writes There and Back through a childhood, a flight, and a return, opening with father, child, and nurse, a stepmother and nurse, and the flight itself. A bookbinder and his pupil, the Mansons, Simon Armour, comparisons, a lost shoe, a holiday, and a library follow, with Alice, Mortgrange, a beech-tree, and the library again. Barbara Wylder, Barbara and Richard, Barbara and others, and Mrs Wylder carry the middle chapters.

Barbara and her critics, the parson's parable, the Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a human gadfly. Richard with Wingfold and his wife deepen the story, before Richard and Alice, a sister, Barbara and Lady Ann, and Alice and Barbara close the circle. MacDonald's novel moves, as its title promises, out into the world and back to faith and home. Readers of his Scottish fiction will find the familiar blend of realism, fairy-tale echo, and moral seriousness.
8953-the-norsk-nightingale-being-the-lyr:
William F. Kirk published this comic book in 1905, in the voice of a Norwegian lumberjack, or lumberyack, in the American North Woods. The lyrics are written in stage dialect, with a Swede's tangled English, and they sing of Yim, Tillie Olson, Little Steena, and the daily life of the camps. Kirk then adds his own comic retellings of history.

Horatius at the Bridge, William Tell, Robinson Crusoe, and Paul Revere all get the lumberjack treatment, as do famous poems such as The Charge of the Light Brigade and Psalm of Life. The jokes rest on dialect and on high tales told low. Today the book is both a period jest and a record of immigrant humor.
9483-the-story-and-song-of-black-roderic:
Dora Sigerson wrote The Story and Song of Black Roderick in 1906, a tale in prose and verse of an Irish earl's pride and fall. Black Earl Roderick rides south at dawn with a hundred knights, stern and silent, on his wedding day. His pride, his bitter heart, and a love that comes late shape the tale. Sigerson tells it as both story and song, in a Celtic, legendary voice.

Roderick faces threatened ruin, then a strange and wonderful rescue, as love softens his harsh brow. The verse refrains echo his ride and his fate, lending the tale a ballad's spell. A reader gets a short, haunting Irish romance, rich in pride, doom, and grace, from a poet steeped in her land's lore.
9547-the-cruise-of-the-dry-dock:
T. S. Stribling wrote The Cruise of the Dry Dock in 1917, a sea adventure of war and wonder. A dry dock, a huge floating yard, breaks loose and drifts into strange waters, with a young hero named Caradoc aboard. Chapters promise a mystery ship, a sea serpent, a submarine chase, and a battle. Herbert Morton Stoops drew the pictures, which show the dock under a schooner's shadow.

Caradoc wins his fight, takes command, and faces nerve against gunpowder as the Vulcan returns. The tale mixes modern war craft with old sea romance. A reader gets a rousing boys' adventure of the Great War era, full of pluck, peril, and the open sea.
9925-black-jack:
Max Brand's 1922 western opens in Garrison City, a little cattle town, where Vance Cornish lights his pipe while his sister Elizabeth watches from a hotel window. Elizabeth is in town on a cattle-buying trip, and gunfire soon breaks the drowsy peace of the street.

Brand builds his story from that gunfight outward, through cattle country, quarrels, and dangers, in his fast, plain style. Vance and Elizabeth, brother and sister, face a West where a sleepy town can turn violent in a moment. Readers get a brisk western of cattle, guns, and family loyalty.
9967-mr-waddington-of-wyck:
May Sinclair's 1921 novel opens in a garden room where Fanny Waddington drifts in and out, bringing tulips, white, pink, and red, for flowered Lowestoft bowls. Barbara, making a Stores list of glass towels and puppy biscuits, watches her with a mixture of fondness and worry.

Mr. Waddington of Wyck himself stands at the center of a domestic story about marriage, family, and the quiet strains of English middle-class life. Sinclair writes with psychological care, attentive to small gestures. Readers get a subtle, observant novel, where a bowl of tulips can carry a whole marriage.
a-selection-from-the-lyrical-poems-of-ro:
Robert Herrick's lyrical poems are gathered here in a selection arranged by Francis Turner Palgrave, who also wrote the introduction. The preface gives Herrick's dates, born 1591 and died 1674, and admits that choosing from so many fine pieces invites argument. Herrick was a country parson who wrote like a man in love with the world.

The poems praise Corinna's going a-Maying, daffodils, cherries, country fairs, and brief youth, and the famous counsel to gather rosebuds while time allows. Others turn graver, on death, prayer, and parting. Short, musical, and clear, the lyrics mix pagan delight in the senses with Christian faith, a blend that keeps Herrick read after three centuries.
arrian-anabasis-alexander-chinnock:
Arrian wrote the Anabasis of Alexander around 150 CE, drawing on eyewitness sources. E. J. Chinnock's 1884 translation presents the fullest surviving account of the conquest. Alexander's expedition opened the wonders of the East to the West.

Seven books trail the Macedonian army from Greece to India. Battles, sieges, river crossings, and mutinies unfold in campaign order. Arrian, himself a general and governor, judges Alexander's generalship professionally. He used Ptolemy and Aristobulus, officers who marched with Alexander, as sources. Chinnock's translation keeps the sweep of the march in classic prose. No other ancient account of Alexander matches its completeness and authority.
arrian-anabasis-chinnock:
Arrian, a Greek officer and historian of the Roman era, wrote the Anabasis of Alexander in the second century. E. J. Chinnock translated its seven books into English. Arrian drew on eyewitness accounts now lost to us.

He follows Alexander from his first battles in Asia to his death. Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela, and the march into India unfold in order. Arrian writes as a soldier judging another soldier's craft. Historians still treat his account as the best ancient source on Alexander. Chinnock's version remains plain, steady, and highly readable. Chinnock's translation first appeared in 1884 and long stayed in print.
billy-and-the-big-stick:
Richard Harding Davis sets Billy and the Big Stick in Haiti. Its president, Hamilear Poussevain, called President Ham, revokes the Wilmot Electric Light Company's concession. The company had dared ask payment for lighting Port-au-Prince. Barefoot soldiers surround the power-house. Young Billy Grant, the company's man on the spot, must fight the republic with a cable office and his wits.

Billy warns a Haitian official that he will deliver a copy of his protest to his president first, and returns to the power-house with faithful retainers in tow. Davis, the era's most famous war correspondent, wrote the story as a comic gloss on Roosevelt's big-stick diplomacy. Its Haiti is stage scenery, but the pacing is pure Davis.
by-sheer-pluck: By Sheer Pluck, G. A. Henty's Ashanti War tale. The plucky hero. This book preserves that adventure. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-van-d:
Abraham van Diepenbeeck was an erudite painter of the Flemish school, born at Bois-le-Duc in 1599 and dead at Antwerp in 1675. After a classical education he became one of Rubens's finest pupils and assistants, handling mythological and historical subjects and portraits with skill and vigour. A sound colourist, he moved to Antwerp about 1629, first winning notice painting on glass, including Acts of Mercy windows in the cathedral.

Admitted to the painters' guild in 1638, he directed the academy from 1641. After a visit to Italy he worked chiefly in oil and illustration. His fifty-eight designs for the Abbe de Marolles' Tableaux du Temple des Muses were engraved by Cornelis Bloemaert. In England under Charles I he painted the Duke of Newcastle's family and illustrated his book on horsemanship. His works hang in the Louvre, Vienna, Munich, Dresden, Berlin, and Brussels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoon-anthon:
Flemish portrait painter Anthony van Dyck, born at Antwerp in 1599 and dead in London in 1641, was the seventh child of a silk and linen merchant. Placed as a boy in the studio of Hendrick van Balen, he developed fast. He painted a likeness of an old man at fourteen and a series of heads later revealed in a lawsuit. Before twenty, in 1618, he was admitted to the membership of the Guild of St. Luke at Antwerp, an unusual honour for so young a painter.

The tradition that he was Rubens's apprentice is dismissed here: he was already a master when he entered Rubens's studio to help with decorative work. The entry traces his early Antwerp years, his precocious skill, and his place among Rubens's young assistants, before his English court career. Readers get a careful sorting of legend from record in a short, brilliant life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bismarck:
Bismarck, a diocese in North Dakota, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Erected on the last day of 1909 and suffragan to St. Paul, Minnesota, it covers eighteen counties across 42,316 square miles of prairie. Vincent Wehrle, a Swiss Benedictine of Einsiedeln, became its first bishop in 1910.

Born at Berg in Switzerland in 1855, professed in 1876, and ordained in 1879, Wehrle had laboured among German settlers in the Dakotas before his election. The entry lists parishes, clergy, and schools of a young frontier diocese. It reads as a founding snapshot of Catholic life on the northern plains.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-john-:
Blessed John Ruysbroeck, surnamed the Admirable Doctor, foremost of the Flemish mystics, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Ruysbroeck near Brussels in 1293, he died at Groenendael in 1381. A devout mother trained him from infancy, and at eleven he left home without warning for his uncle John Hinckaert, canon of St. Gudule's at Brussels.

Writing in the Flemish tongue against heretical books spread among the people, he moved with two friends to the hermitage of Groenendael in 1343. Disciples flocked there until the hermitage became a community of canons regular in 1349. His Sparkling Stone and Adornment of the Spiritual Marriage remain classics of mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chevalier-de-:
An entry on Jean-Baptiste de Lamarck, the French botanist, zoologist, and natural philosopher known as the Chevalier de Lamarck. Born at Bazentin in Picardy in 1744, he joined the French army in 1761 after his father's death. He was made an officer on the field during the Seven Years' War. Illness forced him out at twenty-four, and he worked as a bank clerk in Paris while studying medicine and plants.

Lamarck never practised medicine, and his writings on weather and chemistry carry no scientific weight. In biology he excelled: able botanist from 1778, zoologist from 1794, and from about 1800 a speculative writer on the variation of species. His Flore française of 1778 gave the first full account of French plants and set out his dichotomous system, a key that sorts species by paired choices. He held that classification must weigh all parts of a plant, not one alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-communion-of-:
Patrick Morrisroe's entry covers Communion of the sick, which differs from ordinary Communion in persons, dispositions, place, and ceremonies. The Church, anxious for her children's spiritual welfare, will not leave the ill without the sacrament's consolations. Pastors must meet the desires of the dangerously sick, who need strength for the final struggle. They must also meet those who cannot keep the paschal precept in church. They must meet all who hunger for this life-giving bread from mere devotion.

Dispositions get their own section. The sick who receive from devotion were bound to fast beforehand. Ceremonies follow the Roman Ritual, with the priest bearing the sacrament to the house. Morrisroe draws on Catalani, Baruffaldi, O'Kane, Van der Stappen, and Gasparri to set out the rules. The entry serves pastors and families facing illness, showing how the Church brings the altar to the bedside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-croagh-patric:
This entry describes Croagh Patrick, the cone-shaped mountain on Clew Bay in County Mayo, called the Sinai of Ireland. Rising 2,510 feet above the Atlantic shore, it was known in pagan times as Cruachan Aigli. Its Christian fame rests on St. Patrick's Lent there in 441.

Weary from labour, Patrick climbed the peak on the Saturday before Ash Wednesday to fast, pray, and plead that faith might not fail in Ireland. Tradition tells that God summoned all Ireland's saints, past, present, and future, to console him with a vision of the harvest his work would yield. The entry warns that its sources postdate Patrick by three hundred years, yet argues the traditions they carry are genuine. Pilgrimage continues there to this day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-rock:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Rock, antiquarian and ecclesiologist, born at Liverpool in 1799 and dead at Kensington in 1871. Schooled at Saint Edmund's College, Old Hall, he came under the liturgist Louis Havard and befriended the historian Mark Tierney. Chosen among the first students to reopen the English College at Rome, he took a doctorate there in 1825.

Ordained in 1824, he served at Saint Mary's, Moorfields, then as chaplain to the Earl of Shrewsbury at Alton Towers. His Hierurgia of 1833, on the sacrifice of the Mass, grew from two Roman years of research. His greatest book, The Church of Our Fathers, studies the Sarum Rite and medieval liturgy, and made him England's leading authority on the subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eberhard-bill:
Eberhard Billick, also called Steinberger, was a German theologian and foe of the Reformation, born at Cologne in 1499 or 1500. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows him into the Carmelites in 1513, through vows, priesthood, and a readership in divinity, to the priorships of Cassel and Cologne. He took his doctorate in 1540 and in 1542 became provincial of Lower Germany, a post he held until death, though named auxiliary bishop of Cologne too late to be consecrated.

His work for his order thrived, enrolling many candidates, and his writing against Bucer drew the wrath of Luther and Melanchthon. Disputations took him to Worms, Ratisbon, and Augsburg, and in 1551 he attended the Council of Trent as theologian to Cologne's new archbishop. He died at Cologne on 12 January 1557.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edelinck:
Edelinck is the family name of four engravers, chief among them Gerard Edelinck. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Gerard, born at Antwerp about 1640, learned the rudiments from Galle and drank in the vigor of the Rubens school of engravers. Paris drew him in 1665, where study with de Poilly soon left the master behind and brought him almost at once to his full powers.

Le Brun and Colbert drew Louis the Fourteenth's eye to him. From the king came commissions, a pension, the title of royal engraver, Gobelins rooms, and a professorship there. He pictured the king's features in fourteen engravings, and his powers stayed undimmed until his death at Paris in 1707.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-and-p:
Francis and Peter Kenrick were brothers, Dublin-born archbishops who shaped the Catholic Church in nineteenth-century America, Francis at Baltimore and Peter at St. Louis. Francis Patrick, born 3 December 1797, and Peter, born 17 August 1806, were sons of Thomas Kenrick and Jane. Their uncle, Father Richard Kenrick of St. Nicholas of Myra, Dublin, nurtured the piety he saw early in both boys. At eighteen Francis was chosen to study for the priesthood at Rome, where the gentle bearing of the restored Pius VII left a lasting lesson.

Francis threw himself into Scripture and the Fathers, and his learning later served the American Church against the Nativist and Know-Nothing attacks of his day. Peter built up the vast St. Louis diocese, riding hundreds of miles on visitation and bringing in religious orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-ove:
Friedrich Overbeck, a convert painter born at Lübeck in 1789, led the Nazarene school that remade German religious art. Trained at the Vienna Academy, he quit its formalism and settled at Rome in 1810 with three friends in the empty Irish Franciscan house of San Isidoro. He held that church art had stalled for three centuries and set out to bridge the gap.

His Joseph frescoes at Casa Bartholdi, his Tasso scenes at Villa Massimo, and his Miracle of Roses at Assisi won praise for fresh technique and for fitting painting to architecture. His Triumph of Religion in the Arts still hangs at Frankfurt's Städel Gallery. Through pupils like Steinle, and through France, Belgium, Poland, and Spain, his spirit spread well beyond Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-leo-ha:
George Leo Haydock, a priest and Biblical scholar born in Lancashire in 1774, gave English Catholics their enduring Douay Bible. Schooled at Douai, he fled the Revolution in August 1793 with his brother Thomas and reached Crook Hall by 1796. Ordained in September 1798, he served poor missions at Ugthorpe and Whitby, then Westby Hall, where a clash with superiors cost him his faculties in 1831.

Eight years of study at the Tagg followed, with two appeals to Rome intercepted, until a third appeal in 1838 restored him and sent him to Penrith for his last decade. His chief work re-edited Challoner's text of the English Vulgate, issued at Manchester in 1812 to 1814 and reprinted into the 1850s. He also wrote The Tree of Life, prayer books, hymns, and Sabbath meditations, leaving further biblical manuscripts unpublished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giles-de-coni:
Giles de Coninck, also called Regius, was a Jesuit theologian born at Bailleul in French Flanders in 1571, who died at Louvain in 1633. He entered the Society of Jesus at twenty-one and studied at Louvain under Lessius. He then succeeded his teacher in the chair of scholastic theology, which he held for eighteen years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article praises his concise, clear, and direct style.

St. Alphonsus ranked him a moral theologian of distinction, though de Lugo attacked his views on many points. His chief work, a commentary and disputations on the whole teaching of St. Thomas, appeared at Antwerp in 1616 and ran through many editions. A later Rouen edition was condemned to be torn and burnt by the parliament there in 1762. His treatise on the morality of supernatural acts and his posthumous disputations round out his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-bruc:
Mainz bishop Heinrich Brück, born at Bingen in 1831, rose from the cooper's trade to the chair of church history and the episcopate. Taught by Dr. Hirschel, trained at Mainz seminary, ordained in 1855, and polished at Munich under Döllinger and in Rome, taught church history at Mainz from 1867. He taught there except during the seminary's closure from 1878 to 1887.

Canon in 1889 and bishop in 1899, he ruled Mainz with zeal until 1903. His fame rests on books. A church history manual of 1874 was translated into English, French, and Italian. A five-volume history of the Catholic Church in Germany in the nineteenth century was praised for thoroughness and sound judgment. Beside them stand lives, a study of rationalism, and a study of Spain's secret societies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-wang:
Munich Jesuit Heinrich Wangnereck, born in 1595, taught philosophy and theology at Dillingen for most of his life and served as its chancellor for twenty-four years by one account. Entering the Society at sixteen at Landsberg, he also taught the lowest gymnasium class and preached widely. He spent 1655 to 1660 as superior and missioner at Lindau before returning to Dillingen, where apoplexy at table killed him in 1664.

Princes, bishops, and prelates across Germany sought his advice, and twenty known works, chiefly theological, include a 1630 commentary on St. Augustine's Confessions still popular in a fourth edition of 1907. He also entered the political controversies of his day, once punished by his general for speaking disrespectfully of the Duke of Bavaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hubert-and-ja:
Hubert and Jan van Eyck were Flemish brothers, illuminators and painters who founded the school of Bruges and thus all the painting schools of northern Europe. Hubert was born at Maeseyck about 1366, and Jan about twenty years later. Their sister Margaret won fame as a miniaturist. The earliest mention of a Hubert painting dates to 1413.

Hubert lived at Ghent by 1424 and died there in 1426. Jan presented a Madonna's head to Antwerp's guild in 1420, decorated a paschal candle for Cambrai in 1422, and served Jean Sans Merci at The Hague in 1425. Later he joined Philip the Good of Burgundy as painter and chamberlain. He travelled to Portugal to paint Isabella's portrait true to life for Philip's marriage choice, and settled at Bruges, where his art reshaped northern painting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-chadwic:
Second bishop of Hexham and Newcastle, James Chadwick was born at Drogheda, Ireland, on 24 April 1813, and died at Newcastle on 14 May 1882, buried at Ushaw. His father John Chadwick was a gentleman of an old Catholic Lancashire family settled in Ireland, and his mother was Frances Dromgoole. He was educated at Ushaw College from May 1825 until his ordination on 17 December 1836.

Ushaw kept him for years after ordination: three as general prefect, then as teacher of humanities, then five years as philosophy professor. The vice-presidency of the college and the chair of dogmatic theology came in 1849, but within a few months his health broke down. Recovery came among secular priests devoted to preaching missions and retreats, and after fire destroyed their Wooler house in 1856 he returned to Ushaw as philosophy professor. The entry follows a college man toward the episcopate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-eck:
Johann Eck, theologian and Luther's chief adversary, was born at Eck in Swabia in 1486 and died at Ingolstadt in 1543. His family name was Maier, his father a town magistrate, and Johann took Eckius from his birthplace after 1505. His uncle at Rothenburg schooled him from 1495.

Admitted to Heidelberg at twelve, Eck took arts master's at Tübingen in 1501. He studied at Cologne and Freiburg, adding law, physics, maths, geography, Hebrew, and Greek to philosophy and theology. Tutoring his way after his uncle cut funds, he became rector of Freiburg's arts hall in 1505. He took bachelor of theology, lecturer on the Sentences, licentiate in 1509, and doctor at twenty-four in 1510, ordained in 1508.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-alcock:
John Alcock was an English bishop, statesman, and builder who founded Jesus College, Cambridge. Born at Beverley in 1430, he studied at Cambridge, held the rectory of St. Margaret's in London and the deanery of St. Stephen's, Westminster, and became Master of the Rolls in 1462 and privy councillor in 1470. He served on commissions treating with Scotland and was tutor to the young King Edward V.

As bishop successively of Rochester, Worcester, and Ely, he restored many church buildings and was buried in a fine chapel he had built for himself in Ely Cathedral. His writings include the Sponsage of a Virgin to Christ, the Hill of Perfection, sermons on Luke's eighth chapter, and translations from the French. Bale praised his virtue and sanctity, and he founded Jesus College on the site of a ruined nunnery, endowing Peterhouse as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mullock:
John Mullock was the Franciscan Bishop of St. John's, Newfoundland, who championed its fisheries, resources, and the Atlantic cable. Born at Limerick in 1807, he studied at Seville and at St. Isidore's in Rome, where he was ordained in 1830, served long in Ireland, and became coadjutor of St. John's in 1847, succeeding Bishop Fleming in 1850.

Under him the Church grew rapidly, a new diocese of Harbour Grace was erected, and the splendid St. John's cathedral, begun in 1841, was consecrated in 1855. Keen on Newfoundland's commercial development, he advised governors on fisheries and other matters. Long before the first cable attempt of 1857 he publicly argued that Europe and America could be joined by submarine telegraph. He also introduced English readers to St. Alphonsus Liguori with a life in 1846 and a translation of his History of Heresies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-nepomuk-:
John Nepomuk Tschupick was a celebrated Viennese court preacher of the eighteenth century. Born at Vienna in 1729, he entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1744 and soon taught grammar and rhetoric. In 1763 he became preacher at Vienna cathedral, a post he filled for the last twenty-two years of his life, marked by exceptional conscientiousness, prudence, and ability.

His preaching won the high appreciation of Francis I, Maria Theresa, Joseph II, and the imperial court. His sermons stood out for clear, logical thought and precise, forceful expression, and copious, skillful use of patristic and biblical texts. His sermons were collected in ten small volumes with an index at Vienna in 1785 to 1787. They were supplemented by new sermons in 1798 to 1803, re-edited in five volumes at Paderborn, and translated into Italian. They kept his reputation long after his death in 1784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kasper-franck:
Kasper Franck (1543-1584) was a Saxon preacher who began as a fervent Lutheran and ended as a Catholic controversialist at Ingolstadt. This entry traces how talks with the convert Martin Eisengrein turned him, leading to a public profession of the Catholic faith on 25 January 1568.

With a papal dispensation he took priestly orders and worked as a missionary in Haag and Kraiburg, then returned to Ingolstadt University, serving several terms as its rector. A trip to Rome for the 1575 jubilee brought him a theology doctorate from Siena and papal titles. His polemical books argue his change of faith from the early Church fathers, showing wide reading and a sharp eye for detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lawrence-beye:
Lawrence Beyerlinck (1578-1627) was a Belgian theologian and church writer of Antwerp, son of a noted pharmacist. Trained at Louvain for his father's trade, he chose the priesthood instead and was ordained in June 1602.

While still a student he taught poetry and rhetoric at Vaulx, pastored Herent while teaching philosophy nearby, and from 1605 taught philosophy and theology at Antwerp's seminary, later becoming its superior. Canon, censor, and theologian of Antwerp church in 1608 and protonotary in 1614, he preached and wrote without cease. Compilation was his bent: his Magnum Theatrum Vitae Humanae, a seven-volume alphabetical encyclopedia of 1631 ranging from deep theology to trivia, gathered others' material into final form under his hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limerick:
Limerick, in Ireland, is a diocese covering most of County Limerick and part of Clare, about 500,000 acres. St. Patrick visited the district, and St. Senan, once Abbot of Scattery Island, followed him in converting the natives. In the same century St. Munchin, the diocese's patron, founded a monastery and school at Mungret.

Quick to see the place's trade value, they settled there in the ninth century, oppressing the natives and plundering the Shannon's religious houses. Brian Boroihme punished them at the end of the tenth century, expelled them, and readmitted them as Thomond's subjects and tributaries. We do know of a bishop about 1100, Gillebert, educated at Bangor, where he had been abbot. He presided at the Synod of Rathbreasail in 1118, which fixed the Irish dioceses' number and limits and made Limerick subject to Cashel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-rock:
