Little Rock is the Catholic diocese formed in 1843 from Arkansas and the Indian Territory, lands of the Louisiana Purchase. Early church work there was thin: the white population counted under four hundred in 1799, and mission priests from Missouri served scattered settlers and Osage Indians.

Andrew Byrne of New York became the first bishop in 1844, when Catholics in the diocese numbered barely a thousand. He brought Sisters of Mercy from Ireland, who opened academies at Little Rock in 1850 and Fort Smith in 1851. Civil War stalled the work, Byrne died in 1862, and Edward Fitzgerald of Ohio took over in 1867 to rebuild it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lubeck:
Lubeck was a free imperial city and Hanse town, the second smallest and twentieth in population among German Empire states. City and district covered about 115 square miles, with 105,857 people in 1905, mostly Lutherans, with 2,457 Catholics and 638 Jews.

First settled in the eleventh century among Baltic Slavs, then destroyed, it was refounded in 1143 by Count Adolf II. He chose the Trave-Wakenitz junction, with settlers from Flanders, Holland, Westphalia, and Friesland. Henry the Lion gave it a constitution and mint. Frederick Barbarossa confirmed its liberties in 1188, and Danish rule ended with Holstein victory in 1227, leaving Lubeck free and trading across the Baltic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-cleno:
Maurice Clenock, a Welsh churchman who died about 1580, rose high under Mary and fell with her reign. Educated at Oxford, where he took a canon law degree in 1548, he served Cardinal Pole as almoner and secretary. He held York, Orpington, Shoreham, and Croydon posts, and in 1556 became rector of Corwen. Nominated Bishop of Bangor in 1558, he was never consecrated, since Elizabeth's settlement intervened.

Giving up all his preferments, he followed Bishop Goldwell to Rome and the English hospital there. As warden in 1578 he became first rector when Gregory XIII turned the hospital into a college. Cardinal Allen judged him honest and friendly yet unfit to rule. Accused of favouring Welsh students over thirty-three English ones, he faced such heat that murder seemed near, and he was replaced.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-baro:
Melchior von Diepenbrock, Cardinal and Prince-Bishop of Breslau, was born at Bocholt in Westphalia in 1798 and died at Johannisberg in Upper Silesia in 1853. He attended the military academy at Bonn and fought France in 1815 as a militia officer. On returning, he fell under the spell of Johann Michael Sailer, a family friend then teaching at Landshut, and studied public finance there.

When Sailer became Bishop of Ratisbon, Diepenbrock followed, took up theology, and was ordained in December 1823. In 1835 he became cathedral dean and vicar-general. His languages, administrative gifts, deep inner life, and ascetic temper won him Breslau in 1845. He first declined, then accepted in filial obedience to Gregory XVI. Famine in Upper Silesia stirred his generous heart, and the Revolution of 1848 found him facing sectarian pressure backed by state officials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-osnabrueck:
Osnabrueck is a German diocese directly subject to the Holy See, covering the Hanover districts of Osnabrueck and Aurich, bar one port town, plus Hanover west of the Weser. In 1910 it counted 12 deaneries, 108 parishes, 153 mission posts, 271 parish priests, 12 regular priests, and 204,500 Catholics. Its bishop also heads the Northern Missions of Germany.

Charlemagne founded the Gymnasium Carolinum, and similar schools stand at Meppen, Papenburg, and Osnabrueck. Men religious are few, a Capuchin house and a Marist school at Meppen, while women's orders include Benedictines, Borromeans, Franciscans, and Ursulines. The Romanesque cathedral of Saints Crispin and Crispinian, built in the early twelfth century on Charlemagne's wooden church, holds a treasury of medieval art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-lambeck:
Peter Lambeck, usually called Lambecius, was a Hamburg historian and imperial librarian, born in 1628. Tutored at home and at the Johanneum, he came under his uncle Lucas Holstenius, the great philologist, who guided him to Amsterdam, Paris, and two years of research in Rome. At nineteen his critical notes on Aulus Gellius already won Parisian praise. He became professor of history at Hamburg in 1652 and rector in 1664.

Enemies and an atheism charge, with an unhappy marriage, drove him from Hamburg to Vienna. Emperor Leopold made him librarian and court historiographer, and his eight-volume catalogue of the imperial library remains valuable, above all for Old German language and literature. His Prodromus of 1659 was the first chronological history of literature. He died at Vienna in 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plock:
Plock is a Polish diocese in Russian Poland, suffragan, or subordinate, to Warsaw, covering Plock district and parts of Łomża and Warsaw. It was founded about 1087 through legates of Gregory VII and first certainly noticed in 1102. It once stretched between the Vistula, Narew, and Bug across most of Masovia and northern Podlachia.

Its bishops, under Gniezno until 1818 and Warsaw thereafter, held vast estates, 240 villages by a charter of 1239. Those lands were later split with the cathedral chapter and then seized piecemeal by the Russian government. The see stood vacant from 1853 to 1863 and again from 1885 to 1890. It suffered under Russian rule and faced the spread of the Mariavite sect. Recent bishops Szembek and Wnukowski rose to Mohileff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reginald-peco:
Reginald Pecock, Bishop of Chichester, was born in North Wales about 1395 and died at Thorney Abbey about 1460. He studied at Oriel College, Oxford, winning a fellowship in 1417, then taught in the schools of Exeter College and gained a wide name for learning. Ordained priest on 8 March 1421, he took a divinity degree four years later and moved to court, where Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, took him into favour.

In 1431 he became master of Whittington College in London and rector of Saint Michael's in Riola. London Lollard activity drew him into controversy, and he answered with two books: The Book or Rule of Christian Religion and Donet, an introduction to Christian doctrine published about 1440. He was made Bishop of Saint Asaph in 1444, before rising to Chichester, and the entry follows his learning, his writings, and his church career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-von:
Sebastian von Rostock, bishop of Breslau, was born at Grottkau in Silesia on 24 August 1607 and died at Breslau on 9 June 1671. He studied classics at Neisse and philosophy and theology at Olmütz from 1627 to 1633, was ordained in 1633, and served at Neisse, famed for courage and preaching. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a pastor turned restorer of churches.

When Swedes seized Neisse in 1642, Rostock was taken prisoner and carried to Stettin. Freed and ennobled by the emperor, he stayed at Neisse until moving to Breslau cathedral in 1649, then became vicar-general in 1653. Largely through him, the emperor's right of reformation under Westphalia was enforced in Breslau territory. Some 656 Catholic churches seized by Protestants returned to their owners, though finding priests for so many proved hard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seven-branch-:
The seven-branch candlestick ranked among the three chief furnishings of the Holy Place in the Tabernacle and Temple. In truth it was an elaborate lampstand of finest beaten gold, set on the south side so as to face the loaves of proposition. A central shaft bore three pairs of branches curving upward, all richly ornamented, holding seven golden lamps in a line to light the sanctuary.

Priests dressed the lamps in the morning and set them on the stand in the evening. All night the seven lamps burned, while by day, Josephus reports, three were lit. Levites of the family of Caath carried the lampstand on the march. It went among the spoils Vespasian and Titus carried to Rome, and it may still be seen carved on the Arch of Titus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Saint John, New Brunswick, began in 1854 under Bishop Connolly, later Archbishop. Two years earlier he had sent Honora Conway, later Mother Mary Vincent, to the New York Sisters of Charity novitiate to prepare for a local foundation. The cholera epidemic of 1854 left many orphans in Saint John, and Conway returned to lead the new community.

Four other young women soon joined her, and Bishop Connolly drew up rules for the group. Their work covered care for orphans and the aged poor and Christian education of the young. In Saint John they ran a girls' orphanage, a home for the aged, and a boys' industrial school at Silver Falls, and they taught in the public schools. Their mother-house and novitiate stand at Saint John, with houses across the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicholas-p:
Nicholas Pieck, a Franciscan friar martyred at Briel in 1572, led the nineteen Martyrs of Gorkum. Born at Gorkum in Holland on 29 August 1534 to devout parents, he studied at Bois-le-Duc, joined the Friars Minor, and was ordained priest in 1558. He preached through Holland and Belgium, combating Calvinist teaching and strengthening Catholics.

Made guardian of his native convent, he warned his townsmen as Calvinist forces threatened Gorkum. Captured with his companions, he was carried to Briel and hanged on 9 July 1572 for refusing to deny the Eucharist and papal primacy. The entry praises his open, genial bearing and singular humility. It offers a compact life of a pastor killed in the Dutch wars of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-patrick:
Patrick, apostle of Ireland, was carried from Britain as a teenage slave and returned as a missionary bishop. Born at Kilpatrick near Dumbarton in 387 to Calphurnius and Conchessa, he was seized by Irish raiders at sixteen and sold to Milchu in Antrim. Six years herding flocks on Slemish deepened his prayer, and after escape he trained under Germanus of Auxerre.

Sent by Celestine I after Palladius failed, he landed in Ireland and preached, baptised, ordained clergy, and founded churches across the island. The entry sifts his Confession and Letter against later legend, weighs the dates of his death, 460 or 493, and surveys his lasting mark on Irish faith. It remains the fullest reference life of Ireland's patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-simon-stoc:
Simon Stock, sixth general of the Carmelites, is honoured as the order's most celebrated leader. Born in Kent about 1165, also called Simon Anglus, he is said to have lived as a hermit in a hollow oak at twelve. He later preached as an itinerant before joining the Carmelites newly come to England. Tradition sends him to Rome and Mount Carmel for several years.

What is historically certain begins in 1247, when he was elected general at Aylesford, succeeding Alan. Despite great age he showed remarkable energy, spreading the order through southern and western Europe. He founded houses in university cities: Cambridge in 1248, Oxford in 1253, Paris and Bologna in 1260. He died at Bordeaux on 16 May 1265, famed for the Brown Scapular devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-august:
Thomas Augustine Hendrick, first American bishop of Cebu in the Philippines, was born at Penn Yan, New York, in 1849. Ordained priest at St. Joseph's Seminary, Troy, in 1873, he spent twenty-nine years in parish work in the Diocese of Rochester. There he took a leading part in public and charitable work, and served on the board of regents of the State University.

After the Spanish-American War, when the Church in the Philippines was reorganized, he was named Bishop of Cebu and consecrated in Rome in 1903. He took possession of the see in March 1904 and worked to restore order and discipline across a large diocese. He died of cholera at Cebu in November 1909.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-sedgwi:
Thomas Sedgwick, a theologian of the English Reformation, held high university posts and lost them all under Elizabeth. Regius professor of divinity at Cambridge in 1557 and rector of Stanhope and vicar of Gainford in 1558, he was stripped of all three soon after Elizabeth came to the throne. From 1562 to 1570 he was confined within ten miles of Richmond, Yorkshire, and then sent to prison at York, where he died in 1573.

Earlier he had disputed with Bucer in 1550, and with Cranmer, Latimer and Ridley in April 1554, when Oxford made him Doctor of Divinity. An unfriendly observer in 1562 called him learned but not very wise. The entry lists his many preferments, most given up before Mary's death, and traces a career broken by the religious settlement.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-triple-candle:
A church ornament used only in the office of Holy Saturday, also called the reed, tricereo, arundo, triangulum or lumen Christi. Its three candles are lit one after another, as the ministers move up the church, from the fire consecrated in the porch. At each lighting the deacon sings "Lumen Christi" and the assistants answer "Deo gratias".

The Missal rubrics treat the instrument as three candles fixed for the occasion to a reed or wand, not as permanent furniture. Brass candlesticks with long handles are often used in practice. Barbier de Montault reads the rubric as setting one candle higher than the others, so the three flames form a triangle. Greek bishops use triple and double candlesticks to bless the people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Innsbruck's university, officially the Royal Imperial Leopold Francis University, began in a college opened in 1562 by Peter Canisius. Emperor Ferdinand I of Austria founded it at his request, carrying out a long-cherished plan to bring higher learning to the people of Tyrol. The imperial edict of foundation was read out in every pulpit in Tyrol on 12 May 1562. The school opened under the Jesuits on 24 June as a gymnasium teaching elements, grammar, and syntax.

A fifth and lowest class followed in 1566, and in 1599 Ferdinand wished the programme widened to a studium universale. The entry traces that widening, the university's faculties, its Jesuit and later state direction, and its scholars. It gives a compact history of a school that grew from a Jesuit college into the university of the Tyrol.

Rostock's university in Mecklenburg-Schwerin was founded in 1419 through the joint efforts of Dukes John IV and Albert V. Pope Martin V granted its bull of foundation on 13 February of that year. At first it held only the three secular faculties, with theology added in 1432 under Eugenius IV. The Bishop of Schwerin served as chancellor, an office later held by the Grand Dukes of Mecklenburg.

Most professors came from Erfurt, including the first rector, Petrus Stenbeke. The city endowed the university richly with lands, as did the Bishop of Schwerin, who gave his Rostock house as a residence. Hamburg and Lübeck later added gifts. In 1427 Martin V granted a rare privilege, and the entry follows the university through Reformation, war, and modern growth on the Baltic coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veit-arnpeck:
Veit Arnpeck was a Bavarian historian born at Landshut in 1440, who died in the same city about 1505. Schooled at Amberg and Vienna, he served as parish priest of St Martin's in his native city and as chaplain to Bishop Sixtus. He ranks among the fathers of Bavarian history, and Aventin praised him as one of his most important predecessors.

His writings include the Chronicon Austriacum, running to 1488, the Liber de gestis episcoporum Frisingensium on Freising's bishops, and the Chronicon Baioariorum. The last far surpasses his earlier works, yet it is itself outdone by the plain narrative of the German version, which Arnpeck himself undertook and carried ten years further. The entry gives a brief life of a pioneer Bavarian chronicler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edmund-ca:
Edmund Catherick was a priest and martyr, born probably in Lancashire about 1605, executed at York on 13 April 1642. He sprang from the old Catherick family of Carlton and Stanwick in Yorkshire's North Riding, known for loyalty to the faith. Schooled at Douai College and ordained there, he went to the English mission about 1635 and began a seven-year ministry that ended with his death.

During that ministry he used the alias Huddleston, probably his mother's maiden name. Seized in the North Riding near Watlas, pursuivants brought him before Justice Dodsworth, a connection by marriage, possibly an uncle. Gillow records that admissions made to Dodsworth in seeming friendship convicted Catherick. Arraigned at York and condemned for his priesthood, he suffered in 1642.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-george-ha:
George Haydock was an English martyr born in 1556 and executed at Tyburn on 12 February 1583-84. Youngest son of Evan Haydock of Cottam Hall in Lancashire and Helen Westby of Mowbreck Hall, he studied at the English Colleges of Douai and Rome. He was ordained priest, apparently at Reims, on 21 December 1581. Seized in London soon after landing, he endured a year and three months of the strictest Tower confinement.

During that time he suffered a return of severe malarial fever first caught in the early summer of 1581 while visiting Rome's seven churches. About May 1583, though still in the Tower, his imprisonment eased to free custody, and he could administer the sacraments to fellow prisoners. In his first captivity he adorned his cell with the name of Jesus. Tried and condemned for his priesthood, he suffered at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-wood:
John Woodcock was an English Franciscan martyr born at Leyland in Lancashire in 1603, who suffered at Lancaster on 7 August 1646. Thomas and Dorothy Woodcock, his parents, the latter Catholic, belonged to the middle class. Converted about 1622, he studied a year at Saint-Omer and was admitted to the English College at Rome on 20 October 1629. On 16 May 1630 he joined the Capuchins in Paris.

Soon afterwards he moved to the English Franciscans at Douai. He received the habit from Henry Heath in 1631 and Arthur Bell professed him a year later. For some years he lived at Arras serving as chaplain to Mr Sheldon. Late in 1643 he reached Newcastle-on-Tyne and was arrested on his first night in Lancashire. After two years jailed in Lancaster Castle, he was condemned on his own confession for being a priest and suffered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-nicholas-:
Nicholas Garlick was a priest and martyr born at Dinting in Derbyshire about 1555, who died at Derby on 24 July 1588. He read at Gloucester Hall, now Worcester College, Oxford, matriculating in 1575, but took no degree, perhaps because of the Oath of Supremacy attached to it. He then became master of the high school at Tideswell in the Peak, where his holy influence moved three pupils to follow him to Reims.

One of those pupils, Christopher Buxton, himself became a martyr. Garlick reached Reims in June 1581, took ordination, and returned to England in January 1583. After a year at work, probably in the Midlands, arrest followed, and in 1585 he was exiled, knowing return would bring no mercy. Nevertheless he soon resumed work in the same neighbourhood, was seized by Topcliffe, and suffered at Derby.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-de-buc:
Victor De Buck was a Flemish Bollandist, one of the Jesuit scholars who edited the Acta Sanctorum, the great collection of saints' lives, who lived from 1817 to 1876. Born at Oudenarde to a distinguished family, he studied at Soignies, Roulers. The Jesuit college at Alost, entered the Society in 1835.

After philosophy and science at Namur was summoned, despite his youth, to assist the revived Bollandist work at Brussels. Ordained at Louvain in 1848, he was permanently assigned to the Bollandists in 1850 and laboured there until death, already contributing sixteen unsigned commentaries to the October volume of 1845. Later sections treat his learned controversies, including a study of red-tinted phials, printed in only a few copies for cardinals and prelates, which rumour falsely claimed his superiors had suppressed and destroyed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-john-:
William John Fitzpatrick was a Dublin historian famed for digging up secrets about great men. Born in Dublin in 1830, he died there in 1895. Son of a rich merchant, he had means to feed his bent for biography, above all for facts hitherto unknown and not always welcome. Schooled partly at a Protestant school and partly at Clongowes Wood, he published his first book, on Lord Cloncurry, in 1855.

That same year he charged Sir Walter Scott with plagiarism in the Waverley novels, crediting Scott's brother Thomas, a claim Thomas's daughters rejected. His pen never rested: The Sham Squire of 1866, Ireland before the Union of 1867, O'Connell's correspondence of 1888, and Secret Service under Pitt of 1892. His style repels, but his research, industry, and fair play won praise from both Lecky and Gladstone, and in 1876 he became history professor at the Hibernian Academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-rubru:
William Rubruck was a Franciscan friar whose journey to the Mongol court produced a geographical masterpiece of the Middle Ages. Born at Rubrouc in northern France probably about 1200, he died after 1256. Close to Saint Louis in Paris, he joined the king's crusade and stood at Acre and Tripoli. Louis, hoping to convert the Tatars and win them against the Saracens, sent Rubruck east at his command.

Starting from Constantinople in 1253, Rubruck crossed the Black Sea and Crimea, met Sartach's khan, was passed to Batu on the Volga, then to Great Khan Mangu, reaching Karakorum at Easter 1254. He came home empty-handed by Cyprus and Tripoli in spring 1255. His report to the king outstripped all earlier travel books in observation and clarity, describing China, silk, paper money, printing, pulse doctors, and proving the Caspian an inland sea.
doe-osti-2575077-pfas-removal-by-ion-exc: PFAS removal by ion exchange got its Hanford review, and this DOE report covers background and knowledge gaps. The pages detail the resin science. The cleanup crews get their briefing. The site was Hanford. The resins were ion exchange. The science was resin.
doe-osti-2589585-low-swap-trapped-ion-at: Trapped ion atomic clocks got their low SWaP, and this DOE report covers the compact design. The pages detail the engineering. The timing folks get their device. The clock was trapped ion. The design was compact. The folks were timing.
doe-osti-3029333-final-technical-report-: Quantum black holes got finally reported, and this DOE technical report covers wormholes. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their closeout. The report was final technical. The closeout was physicist. The wormholes were holes. The holes were black.
galen-natural-faculties-brock:
Arthur J. Brock translated Galen's On the Natural Faculties for the Loeb series in 1916. Galen, antiquity's greatest doctor after Hippocrates, wrote the treatise around 175 CE. It became the foundational text of ancient physiology for centuries.

Galen holds that each organ has purpose-built powers of its own. The stomach attracts, retains, alters, and expels food by distinct faculties. Kidneys, liver, and blood vessels each work by similar natural powers. His system ruled medicine for some fourteen hundred years afterward. Brock's Loeb gives Greek facing English for students. Modern physiology replaced Galen's faculties, but his reasoning shaped medicine's very questions.
gobseck:
Honore de Balzac's Gobseck, translated by Ellen Marriage, opens at one in the morning in the winter of 1829-30, in the Vicomtesse de Grandlieu's salon, where the lawyer Derville tells a story. Its subject is Gobseck, the Dutch moneylender, a pupil of Balzac's own Vendome schoolfellow's dedication reminds readers, rendered as philosophy with a cash box. Gobseck lends to desperate aristocrats and watches Paris through its debts.

The Countess de Restaud burns papers in the grate as Derville approaches, fearing a will that disinherits her children, while Gobseck savors his one laugh at the expense of the ruined. Balzac returns to Gobseck across the Comedie humaine; this tale is the usurer's fullest portrait, terrifying and oddly admiring.
good-luck: Good Luck, by L, t, meade, the luck's tale. This book preserves that children's story. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
govdocs-archive_org-LiturgicalShipwreck_:
Michael Davies, an English Catholic traditionalist writer, published Liturgical Shipwreck in the 1990s, marking twenty-five years of the reformed Roman Mass, 1969 to 1994. Davies defended the old Latin rite against the changes that followed the Second Vatican Council. His books armed traditionalists worldwide.

He argues that the new Mass broke with the faith the old rite expressed, and that the wreck of the liturgy wrecked belief itself. Davies marshals texts, translations, and the reformers' own words in a lawyerly case. The book is Catholic traditionalism's argument fully made, of record for readers on any side of the liturgy wars.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrookingJack_Br: 'Rest Stop III' by Jack Brooking (Jack Beach): the declassified government document - the work as captured. Subject: government records. A bare holding, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete. From the archive's collection, for researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FrazierJack_Fra: Jack Frazier: the badly garbled letter apparently concerning dental documents and Oswald's contacts. Damaged, but kept, complete. A single letter. An obscure item, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GougglemanTucke:
Murrey Marder reported for the Washington Post that three Americans were still being held in Vietnam. Among them was a former official of the Central Intelligence Agency. A fourth American had reached Bangkok, which is how word of the others came out.

Men held after a war ends become a slow diplomatic wound. Families wait, governments negotiate in private, and newspapers keep the names alive. Marder's article preserves the state of that captivity as the Post reported it, with one man free in Bangkok and three prisoners still inside Vietnam, their names kept before the public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LawrenceJack_La:
In January 1964, the FBI's Pittsburgh office sent this airtel to the Dallas office about Lee Harvey Oswald. The file heading was 'IS-R-Cuba,' the bureau's internal-security label for the Oswald case. Special Agent Leon R. Graben reported his attempts to reach a subject in Charleston, West Virginia.

Airtels were the bureau's fast internal messages, and thousands of them built the Oswald file. Most record small errands like this one: an agent sent to find a person, a visit made, a lead checked. Together they show the scale of the inquiry that followed the assassination, reaching into cities far from Dallas and pulling in people who had only glancing contact with the case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NobleNick_Noble:
Harold Weisberg wrote this letter on January 12, 1976, to a Mr. Noble. Its subjects are practical ones. Weisberg discusses the government documents reproduced in his books, and what transcripts cost him to obtain. He also raises Senator Richard Russell's unrecorded doubts about the official account.

Russell had served on the Warren Commission, and researchers believed he had dissented in private. Weisberg chased that belief for years. The letter to Noble mixes that chase with the bookkeeping of self-publishing: documents bought, pages copied, costs counted. It is a working letter from a man running a one-man research institute out of his house, and it shows both halves of that enterprise.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PickupTruck_Pic:
An FBI report dated December 24, 1963 records an account by J. D. LeFlore. LeFlore described a green Chevrolet pickup truck seen stopped in front of the Texas School Book Depository before the motorcade arrived. The truck carried lettering for 'air conditioning' on its side.

Witness reports of strange vehicles fill the early assassination files. Each was logged, however small, because no one yet knew which details mattered. A lettered truck in front of the building an hour before the shooting was exactly the sort of thing agents were told to chase. The report preserves LeFlore's description, the date it was taken, and the bureau's decision to keep it in the record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WaiteJack_Waite: A letter reached Harold Weisberg from Philadelphia on October 20, 1966. The writer mentions work under way and the rechecking of facts. Weisberg drew letters from readers and fellow researchers across the country as his books appeared. The Philadelphia letter is one piece of that early network, when assassination research still moved mostly by mail between people who had never met.
guy-garrick: Arthur B. Reeve's Guy Garrick novel follows a young crime scientist returned from abroad, testing new methods on a wave of motor thefts worth over a million dollars. Garrick tracks a motor bandit gang through gambling dens, blackmail and a siege, using the detectaphone, vocaphone and other listening devices. The chase runs from a stolen motor to a manhunt, a frame-up and a final raid.
joe-the-hotel-boy-or-winning-out-by-pluc:
Joe the Hotel Boy, or Winning Out by Pluck, is a boys' novel by Horatio Alger Jr. The contents run to thirty chapters, from Out in a Storm to a closing Conclusion. In his preface, Alger recalls his long series about boys who make their own way in the world. Newsboys, match boys, peddlers, and street musicians filled the earlier books.

Joe's story turns on a search for a blue box, named again and again in the chapter titles. Along the way come a ruined home, an accident on the lake, a swindle, and a fire at the hotel. Joe visits Chicago, makes a discovery, and sees two evildoers meet their fate. Alger's formula holds: pluck, honesty, and hard work carry a poor boy upward.
master-humphrey-s-clock:
Charles Dickens built Master Humphrey's Clock round an old man and his clock. He gave the book to the poet Samuel Rogers in 1840. His first note to readers is dated April 4, 1840.

Master Humphrey hopes all sorts of readers find cheer in his clock. Dickens says the parts would come out week by week. He trusts the clock's voice to lighten the hours it counts. The frame lets friends meet, tell tales, and share the passing time. A preface to the first volume follows the short address. Dickens frames short tales as gifts left in an old man's clock case.
mistress-penwick:
Dutton Payne's romance opens, by its contents, as the Ursuline convent loses a pupil. The Lord of Crandlemar and a ball follow, then his lordship's proposal. Janet's philosophy and a chapter called The Brantle deepen the intrigue. Sir Julian Pomphrey and a Jacques Dempsy enter the cast.

Later chapters move between castle and ancient monastery. Something happens in the butlery, and nine tolls from the chapel belfry. Sermons new and old close the contents list. Payne builds a tale of convent girlhood, aristocratic courtship, and old buildings full of secrets, in the manner of the period's historical romances.
mr-prohack:
Arnold Bennett's novel follows Arthur Charles Prohack, a calm man who hates to be hurried. Chapter one, The New Poor, finds him at breakfast at eight thirty. The contents promise law, family strain, idleness, and a yacht. Two children, Charlie and Sissie, share the stage with his wife Eve.

Bennett traces how new wealth and new poverty test one household. Prohack tries rest, travel, and doing nothing at all. Eve and the children pull him back into real life. The tone is wry and close to daily detail. It is a study of money, work, and middle age in modern London.
mr-waddington-of-wyck:
May Sinclair published this novel in 1921, set at Lower Wyck Manor. Fanny Waddington drifts in and out with tulips for old bowls. She hums as she works and seems light as a butterfly. Young Barbara Madden watches her during her first days there.

Barbara is new to the house and learns its ways fast. She notes the Tudor windows, the garden, and the stores lists. Mr. Waddington of the title rules this calm world. Sinclair studies marriage and self-deceit in a quiet key. Small acts and soft talk reveal the strain beneath the manor's peace.
nasa-tm-19700024994-crew-egress-procedur:
Dated December 7, 1966, this Houston working paper gives crew escape procedures for the Apollo Block I command module at sea. After a splashdown or a pad abort into water, the crew had to get out of the floating capsule.

The paper opens with a summary and an introduction. It then lays out the steps for leaving the craft in the open sea. Block I capsules were an early design used for ground and early flight tests. Clear escape steps, written before flight, gave crews a practiced path out. That mattered most when a capsule sat low in rough water.
on-horseback:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote this travel book about the South. The ride begins at Abingdon in southwest Virginia. A professor gives a comic lesson on mounting a horse. The horse steps around and faces him mid lesson. Townsfolk watch from cane chairs before the hotel.

Warner rides through North Carolina and East Tennessee. The professor can recite Chaucer's tales while trotting, Warner jokes. Abingdon keeps old tobacco wealth and easy habits, he notes. Warner mixes humor, scenery, and social comment. The book preserves Southern life after the Civil War. The town holds the Stonewall Jackson Institute in its midst. The late Floyd home now serves as a school for girls.
on-the-track:
Henry Lawson published these Australian stories in Sydney in 1900. His preface is dated March 17 of that year. Many tales first ran in various periodicals, he notes. Several appear in print here for the first time. The contents name swagman Mitchell in many tales.

Stories treat matrimony, jobs, women, and old mates. A ventriloquial rooster and bush cats add dry humor. The first tale recalls songs sung on the diggings. Lambing Flat and Gulgong name old gold rush camps. His tales voice Australia's frontier with humor and heartbreak. The contents also list Andy Page's Rival and the Iron-Bark Chip. Home Rule joins the list of old diggings named.
orange-and-green-a-tale-of-the-boyne-and:
G. A. Henty set his boys' novel Orange and Green in the Irish war of 1689 to 1691, when the deposed King James fought William of Orange for the crown. The story runs from a shipwreck through the siege and relief of Derry, the battle of the Boyne, and the sieges of Limerick, ending in peace. Orange and green name the two camps, Protestant and Catholic Irish.

In his preface Henty explains the grievance behind the war: Irish land taken from its owners and given to Cromwell's followers, and what remained preyed on by greedy intriguers. He says he drew most heavily on Irish accounts so his young readers would see events from the Irish point of view. The novel mixes that history lesson with cavalry raids, winter quarters, and dangerous missions.
passing-of-the-third-floor-back:
Jerome K. Jerome's story opens on a November afternoon near Bloomsbury Square in London. A stranger with an odd, curved back and a young face draws the notice of everyone he passes, a newsboy, a nursemaid, and a constable. Copyrighted in 1904, the tale became one of Jerome's best-loved works.

The stranger takes the shabby third-floor back room in a boarding house full of selfish, quarrelling lodgers. His quiet presence slowly changes each of them for the better. Gentle and a little mystical, the story suggests that one good person can redeem a whole household.
peshitta-new-testament-murdock:
James Murdock, an American scholar of Syriac, published his English New Testament from the Syriac Peshitta in 1852. The Peshitta is the Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches of the East, in use since the early centuries of the faith. Murdock's was the earliest widely used English rendering of that version.

Reading the Gospels and letters in Syriac dress gives small shocks: names, phrases, and some whole verses shift from the Greek-based texts most readers know. The Peshitta also lacks a few books found in Western Bibles. Murdock kept notes on the main differences as they came. His version opened the Eastern church's scripture to English readers.
philosopher-jack:
R. M. Ballantyne's Philosopher Jack, dated 1879 in this record, opens with a strange friendship. Jack, whose other name is Edwin, is a nineteen-year-old student of argumentative mind. His most intimate friend never says anything to him beyond two words: Don't, and Do. The friend's name, the reader learns, is Conscience.

A letter from Jack's father then destroys his prospects: bad seasons have emptied the farm purse, and the golden gates of knowledge close. Jack asks himself whether to go to sea, and Conscience says Don't. Ballantyne's tale follows the impulsive philosopher who asks the question anyway: for what end was I created?
podcast-tuckercarlson-2VXbY4V7LCk:
John Mearsheimer, the political scientist known for realist theory and blunt talk, joins Tucker Carlson to argue that Israel's war in Gaza amounts to genocide against Palestinians. His charge goes further: he says the West has been deceived into supporting it, and he names the mechanisms of that deception.

Mearsheimer has criticized American foreign policy for decades, and Carlson gives him an unhurried hearing rare on television. The two discuss media coverage, lobbying, and the strategic cost to the United States. The claims are the speakers' own and remain fiercely disputed, but the episode preserves a prominent scholar making the case directly. Listeners get the argument unfiltered, which is the stated point of the program.
podcast-tuckercarlson-6PdWKkyooCk:
Laura Delano spent years as a psychiatric patient, taking the medications prescribed for her diagnoses, before she concluded the system itself had harmed her. With Tucker Carlson, she argues that the drug industry created the modern mental health crisis and profits from keeping it permanent.

Delano now works with people trying to leave psychiatric drugs safely, and she describes that process and its dangers in detail. Carlson connects her story to his broader case against pharmaceutical power. Her claims are disputed by much of the medical establishment, and withdrawal from such medication carries real risks she herself stresses. The episode preserves a prominent critic's account in her own words, useful for listeners weighing the system's failures against its defenders' answers.
poor-jack:
Captain Frederick Marryat wrote Poor Jack, presented here as volume ten of his collected works with illustrations. Marryat, a post-captain in the Royal Navy turned novelist, knew the sea from boyhood. This story follows a Greenwich waterman's son who rises through the naval world of the Napoleonic wars. The illustration list alone charts the voyage: Fisher's Alley, Anderson reading the Bible to Jack. News of the battle of the Nile, a French port, a prison, an escape, and a wreck.

Jack's father, a disabled pensioner, and old Bramble, the one-legged sailor who mentors the boy, anchor the shore chapters. Marryat mixes dockside comedy with real seamanship, storms, privateers, and impressment, all drawn from life. Poor Jack was among his most popular tales, a boys' classic that also preserves, in its slang and detail, the vanished world of the Thames watermen and the wooden navy.
poor-man-s-rock:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published Poor Man's Rock in Boston with Little, Brown in September 1920, adding it to his shelf of British Columbia novels beside North of Fifty-Three and Big Timber. A prologue reaches back long, long ago, and the chapters settle in Cradle Bay, among salmon fishermen whose living depends on the runs. Titles such as Vested Rights, the Complexity of Simple Matters, and Sea Boots and Salmon announce the fight: small independent fishermen against the cannery interests that claimed the coast.

Sinclair wrote the Pacific Northwest from inside, having fished and logged it himself, and his fiction argues for the little man with the gillnet against companies with lawyers. The rock of the title is the poor man's foothold, a fishing spot the independents could still work. As a document of the salmon wars and as a rattling regional novel, the book holds both grounds at once.
ralestone-luck: Ralestone Luck, by André Norton, author of The Prince Commands, was published in New York by D. Appleton-Century Company in 1938, with illustrations by James Reid, and dedicated to D. B. N. for miles of proofreading. The pages shown give the frontispiece and first contents: Rupert asks Val the old question, "How hold ye Lorne?" and the contents open with The Ralestones Come Home, The Luck of the Lords of Lorne, and Pistols for Two, Coffee for One.
rhymes-of-a-roughneck:
Pat O'Cotter published these rhymes in 1918 and dedicated the book to Alaska, in a verse of rough praise. Alaska is the home of the tin can and dog, he writes, a waste of snow, ice, and moss. Men come there for gold and stick because they cannot get away; they dig, drink, and die.

The contents open with The Birth of the Land and A Woman, A Dog, and A Walnut Tree. The Throwback, The Malamute, and The Prospector name stock figures of the gold country. When the Water Starts to Run and That 30 U.S. on the Wall close the list, in verse as plain and hard as its subject.
struggling-upward-or-luke-larkin-s-luck:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote Struggling Upward, or Luke Larkin's Luck, one of his many tales of a poor boy rising by honesty and pluck. Chapter I, The Waterbury Watch, opens on a January Saturday at a pond in the village of Groveton.

A young teacher, Frederic Hooper, a recent Yale graduate, offers a Waterbury watch as prize to the boy who skates across the pond and back in the least time. Among the racers stands Randolph Duncan. He is the spoiled son of Prince Duncan, the rich bank president. The contest sets the pattern Alger's readers knew. Wealth and pride stand on one side. A deserving poor boy stands on the other. Luck rewards steady conduct.
the-adventures-of-johnny-chuck: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Johnny Chuck. It is one of his Bedtime Story Books. Chapters track Johnny from the spring's first days. Gentle Sister South Wind arrives first. Callers then come to Johnny's door. The singers of the Smiling Pool draw him next. He finds out who the sweet singers are. A bout of discontent then takes him. He turns tramp and meets a strange chuck. Love and house hunting with Polly Chuck follow. A new home at last closes the list.
the-adventures-of-poor-mrs-quack: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Poor Mrs. Quack for his Bedtime Story-Books, with art by Harrison Cady. Chapters listed track Peter Rabbit's first meeting with Mrs. Quack at the Smiling Pool, her tale of home and troubles, the terrible guns on her flight south, a hunt for the lost Mr. Quack, and Sammy Jay's plan to help her.
the-auction-block:
Rex Beach wrote the novel, naming Peter Knight and his son James, called Jimmy, in its first pages. Peter, a plump and good-natured Democrat in the small town of Vale, argues with his son about local politics and reform. James urges a move to New York, while his father insists he likes Vale, where everyone knows him.

That opening clash sets up a story of ambition, family strain, and city temptation. James treats his father's standing as a reason to leave, not to stay. Beach, also named on the title page for The Silver Horde and The Spoilers, builds the tale from small-town talk toward larger stakes in New York life.
the-cruise-of-the-dry-dock: T. S. Stribling's The Cruise of the Dry Dock, dated 1917 with pictures by Herbert Morton Stoops, is dedicated to the author's mother. Its contents promise adventure in twenty-two chapters: The Last of the Vulcan, The Mystery Ship, A Modern Columbus, The Sea Serpent, Chased by a Submarine, and The Victoria Cross. A lad named Caradoc shows his mettle and takes command along the way. The picture list shows the heroes under a schooner's overhang. Only the front matter, contents, and picture list are present here.
the-cuckoo-clock: Mrs. Molesworth, author of Herr Baby and Carrots, wrote The Cuckoo Clock, printed in London by Macmillan in 1895 with pictures by Walter Crane. A dedication dated from Edinburgh in 1877 names Mary Josephine and the dear memory of her brother Thomas Grindal, both called friendly little critics of the author's stories for children. The contents begin with a chapter called The Old House. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-eight-strokes-of-the-clock:
Maurice Le Blanc's The Eight Strokes of the Clock, dated 1923 in its front pages, holds eight Arsène Lupin tales. Le Blanc's note says Lupin told him these feats as a friend's, one Prince Rénine, yet the hero's acts and mind look so much like Lupin's own that the two seem one. Titles name a water bottle, a tell-tale film, and footprints in the snow.

The first tale opens atop a tower, with Hortense Daniel calling down to a fat man in the shrubs. Rénine solves each case with nerve, charm, and a magician's timing.
the-garden-of-the-plynck:
Karle Wilson Baker wrote The Garden of the Plynck as a tale for children, with Sara at its heart. Ten chapters move from a dimple smithy to Sara's day.

The tale opens by teasing grown folk who start tales with when I was a little girl, then turn the tale into a scolding. Sara's mother, dear but busy and contrary, darns, writes, and reads dark books with no pictures. Against that plain world stands the Plynck's garden, a place of odd folk and small wonders. Baker mixes wit for grown readers with a child's world a step off the real one.
the-hunchback:
James Sheridan Knowles wrote the two plays in this volume. The Hunchback and The Love-Chase appear together. Cassell published the edition in 1887. The introduction traces an unlikely career. Knowles was born at Cork in 1784. His father taught elocution and compiled a dictionary. The boy took an army commission. He gave it up for the stage. Acting brought him no greatness. He taught elocution at Belfast and Glasgow instead. His first play appeared at Belfast in 1815.

Everything changed through the actor Macready. Virginius had succeeded at Glasgow. A friend pressed the manuscript on the rising tragedian. Macready read it unwillingly in April 1820. He finished it in a state of excitement. The fresh dialogue and passionate scenes absorbed him. Knowles became Macready's own poet after that. His real gift was building situations for actors. A fine performer could move an audience through them.
the-legends-of-saint-patrick:
Aubrey de Vere wrote verse legends of Saint Patrick first published in 1872, and Cassell issued this small edition in London in 1892. An introduction traces poetic gift from Sir Aubrey de Vere to his third son, born in 1814. Sir Aubrey sonnets won high praise from Wordsworth, the editor notes.

The younger de Vere wrote noble verse tied to love of God, man, and Ireland across a long life. His Patrick legends retell the saint missions, wonders, and prayers in lyric and narrative poems. The editor chose this book from three collected volumes of his verse.
the-life-and-adventures-of-kit-carson-th: De Witt C. Peters wrote his life of Kit Carson from facts Carson narrated himself, and New York publishers issued it in 1858. Only the title page and the start of a dedication letter to Colonel Ceran St. Vrain of New Mexico are present here. The letter calls St. Vrain the first mountaineer to spot and guide Carson energy, ability, and courage. The adventures themselves, across the Rocky Mountains and the far West, remain outside this record.
the-mayor-of-warwick: Herbert M. Hopkins, author of The Fighting Bishop, published The Mayor of Warwick with Houghton, Mifflin and Company in April 1906. Only the title page, a dedication to Pauline, and the contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Chapter titles promise a meeting in the Maple Walk, a bishop's daughter, a candidate, and star-gazers. Later chapters turn to a confession, the president taking a hand, and the blindness of the bishop.
the-moon-rock:
Arthur J. Rees's 1922 novel The Moon Rock opens with an epigraph from Swinburne on a bitter world, then moves to a funeral in Cornwall. Chapter I buries Mrs. Turold in a bleak Cornish churchyard, among strangers and far from her birthplace and kin. The narrator remarks that she had been a nonentity in life and was no less in death.

Her husband lingers alone at the open grave, ignoring the waiting grave-digger. His long, narrow face shows care rather than grief, and his gaze is that of a man sunk in anxious thought. Six mourners wait by a stone cross: four men, a woman, and the dead woman's daughter, whose lovely, sorrowful face turns away from the grave toward the distant sea.
the-norsk-nightingale-being-the-lyrics-o: William F. Kirk published a book of comic verse in 1905, described as the lyrics of a "lumberyack," using Scandinavian immigrant dialect for humor. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. The lyrics include pieces such as "Yim," Tillie Olson, and a sonnet on stewed prunes. The historical tales retell Horatius at the Bridge, William Tell, Robinson Crusoe, and Paul Revere.
the-purgatory-of-st-patrick:
Denis Florence Mac-Carthy translated Calderon's dramas into English in the metre of the original, publishing at London in 1873 with Henry S. King and Company. The introduction singles out Life Is a Dream as the most celebrated of Calderon's plays, staged across Europe and rendered into many languages.

Mac-Carthy stresses completeness and closeness. Every speech is kept, line for line, in the varied verse forms of the Spanish text, improving on earlier partial versions in blank verse or selected scenes. The title drama concerns Saint Patrick's Purgatory, and readers interested in Spanish theatre gain a full metrical rendering rather than a loose adaptation.
the-story-and-song-of-black-roderick:
Dora Sigerson published this Irish tale in prose and verse in 1906. She announces its subject at once. Black Earl Roderick is its hero. The tale covers his pride and his humbling. It covers the bitterness of his heart and the love that reached him at last. His threatened ruin and his strange rescue close the list.

Roderick leaves his gray castle at dawn on his wedding day. A hundred knights ride with him. They go steady and slow, as if to meet sorrow. No man dares sing or jest behind him. Song stanzas describe his heavy frown and sneer. Only Mora of the Knowledge speaks a warning. She picks herbs in a lonely place. She whispers about the white doe he would kill. Then a honeybee stings his cheek on the road.
the-story-of-a-monkey-on-a-stick: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a monkey on a stick was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, with a frontispiece showing the Monkey shaking paws with the Candy Rabbit. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present here. The lists group the book with the Sawdust Doll. The White Rocking Horse and the Calico Clown stand beside it. A Bobbsey Twins list opens after. The monkey's own adventures do not appear.
the-tale-of-jemima-puddle-duck:
Frederick Warne issued Beatrix Potter's Jemima Puddle-Duck in 1908, billed on its opening page as a farmyard tale for Ralph and Betsy. Jemima is annoyed because the farmer's wife will not let her hatch her own eggs. Her sister-in-law Rebeccah cheerfully admits she lacks the patience to brood eggs for nearly a month. Jemima insists she will hatch her eggs all by herself.

She tries to hide her eggs, yet they are always found and carried off, and she grows quite desperate. Potter sets up a determined mother duck against a practical farm household. The opening promises a secret nest, a risky plan, and trouble ahead for a bird who wants things her own way.
the-tapestried-chamber-and-death-of-the-:
Sir Walter Scott frames The Tapestried Chamber as a story told to him years earlier by Miss Anna Seward, whose spoken tales outshone her written ones. The piece first appeared in The Keepsake of 1828. Scott warns that stories of the marvellous lose force in print compared with a voice lowered beside a fireside. He presents the narrative much as he heard it, avoiding ornament that would spoil its simplicity.

The tale itself, also called The Lady in the Sacque, concerns a haunted room in an old house. Scott's introduction doubles as a small essay on why ghost stories work best when told aloud. Readers get both a classic haunting and a great storyteller explaining his craft before the fright begins.
the-wreck:
The Wreck, copyrighted by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1880, opens behind an old farm-house. A girl named Ollie has been swinging in the grove for nearly an hour. Her mother calls her name from the house. Ollie stops the swing and hurries along the path. Mrs. Rogers stands at the back door holding a basket. She has been hunting for Ollie all over the house.

Sugar is what she needs, for new cookies. A recipe from Mrs. Coe uses more sugar than expected. The errand launches the story from a quiet domestic moment. No author is named on the pages shown. Readers meet a country household through a child's small, everyday duties.
the-young-firemen-of-lakeville-or-herber: Frank V. Webster's The Young Firemen of Lakeville, published in 1909, appears here through its front pages and opening contents. Webster's other boys' books are listed for young readers. Titles include Only a Farm Boy and Bob the Castaway. The contents begin with a midnight alarm. Peril follows, and Bert forms a plan. Herbert Dare's pluck is promised in the subtitle. The story chapters themselves start beyond the pages present in this record.
there-back: George MacDonald wrote the novel There and Back, and its contents list runs to forty chapters. Early headings introduce a father, child, and nurse, then a stepmother and a flight. Richard's story moves through a bookbinder, the Mansons, and Simon Armour. Later chapters centre on Barbara Wylder, Alice, Mortgrange, and the parson Wingfold, ending in London. MacDonald's Thomas Wingfold also appears by name in the headings. A contents list alone is shown in this record, so the novel's chapters themselves are not shown.
to-infidelity-and-back:
Evangelist Henry F. Lutz published his religious autobiography at Cincinnati in 1911, subtitled how he found Christ and his church. He dedicated it to pioneers of the nineteenth-century Restoration Movement, who endured poverty and persecution while seeking Christian union on the first, simple gospel. Their beacon light, he says, guided him.

An opening piece, written on his Bible's flyleaf after the struggle, describes emerging from a stormy sea of agony. Sectarianism, rationalism, infidelity, and doubt lacerated his soul. Readers get a truth-seeker's testimony meant for sensitive readers who have endured similar doubt and despair, framed by Isaiah and Bacon.
un-doc-letter-to-un-security-council-by-:
Sir Jeremy Greenstock, Britain's ambassador to the United Nations, sent this letter to the Security Council in 2003, during the crisis over Iraq. The letter put the British position into the Council's formal record. It belongs to the intense diplomacy that ran alongside the debate over war.

In the letter, Greenstock sets out Britain's reading of Iraq's duties under past Council resolutions. He explains why London saw Baghdad as still in breach of those duties. Historians value the letter as a primary record of the British case, stated in Britain's own words at the time.
